full_text:
Jacoby Brissett has struggled to win as a starter, but coaches and teammates throughout his career speak of his reputation as one of the NFL's most respected teammates. Sean M. Haffey / Getty Images
TEMPE, Ariz. — On a late October night in 2018, Andrew Luck drove home after a miserable Sunday afternoon. The Indianapolis Colts had just returned after a 42-34 loss to the New York Jets, dropping their record to 1-5. Luck, the franchise quarterback, could feel himself withdrawing, the last thing a team leader should do.
His cellphone rang. It was Jacoby Brissett.
Brissett, the Colts’ backup quarterback, told Luck he worked too hard. This team was too good. He told Luck he should call a team meeting. Luck was not in a good place, not in a position where he was ready to accept help. He couldn’t help but think: Who does this guy think he is?
The phone conversation lasted 20 minutes. Luck later told his wife about Brissett’s suggestion. Nicole Luck said she thought a team meeting sounded like a good idea. Luck contacted the other team captains.
“And by the third call, my whole demeanor and attitude had shifted,” Luck told The Athletic . “I’m like, ‘My God, Jacoby’s trying to help this team. He’s trying to help me . He’s challenging me.’ And he did it in a really digestible way.”
Everywhere Brissett goes, a similar feeling surfaces: There’s no one better to have in the locker room. Entering his 11th NFL season, the 33-year-old Brissett has played for six teams, which includes two stints with the New England Patriots. This year he is set to quarterback the Arizona Cardinals, the fourth time he will open a season as a starter. It’s been an interesting journey.
Luck calls Brissett not just a good teammate but an “elite” one. Former NFL head coach Bill Parcells, who has known Brissett since the quarterback was a teenager, said Brissett has a special knack for influencing the locker room. Other coaches and teammates, all the way back to Brissett’s college days at North Carolina State, have similar praise.
“He’s always been a leader wherever he’s been,” said Parcells, the Hall of Fame coach and two-time Super Bowl champ. “He just has that ability to round up the people and the charisma to influence them in a positive way. And he’s a dedicated team player that’s just interested in winning. He conveys that, and pretty soon people get to understand him pretty well. He’s just a remarkable young man.”
In a recent conversation, Brissett couldn’t pinpoint what makes him a standout leader. He simply tries to be the same person every day. He recalled the phone call to Luck. He knew how hard Luck had worked to return from the shoulder injury that had kept him out the previous season. He felt like the team needed to hear the determination and drive in Luck’s voice. But most of all, he wanted Luck to know he had his back.
Luck said it’s not uncommon for backup quarterbacks to offer suggestions like this. Earlier in his Indianapolis career, he was fortunate to have Matt Hasselbeck and Drew Stanton in his position room. But that was different, Luck said. Hasselbeck and Stanton were older, wiser. When Brissett suggested the team meeting, he was three years younger than Luck, “and I think for a younger quarterback, (that’s) very rare,” Luck said. After the team meeting, the Colts won nine of 10 to reach the playoffs. The team meeting wasn’t the biggest reason for the reversal, Luck said, but it was a factor.
Former NFL coach Matt Canada saw similar qualities during Brissett’s college days. Brissett began his career at Florida before transferring to North Carolina State, where Canada was offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach. Brissett couldn’t play his first year because of NCAA transfer rules. Nor could he travel with the team for road games. But that didn’t stop Brissett. He traveled on his own dime, often borrowing a friend’s Ford Explorer, to show up and support his teammates.
In the position room that season, Brissett led by example. Each week, Canada would have the quarterbacks turn in their favorite plays. What do you want to run on third-and-3? How would you rank these calls? Brissett turned them in even though he was ineligible to play.
“In coaching, you act like you’re one play away,” Canada said. “You say that to backups and all those things. And it’s real good talk. But Jacoby wasn’t one play away. He was no plays away. He couldn’t play. I’m just saying Jacoby lived it. He literally acted like he was going to start.”
At each stop of his career, Brissett has always found ways to connect with teammates. Once he took over at North Carolina State, Brissett would get on the team bus and hand out personalized, handwritten notes to teammates as he walked to his seat. During his time as Luck’s backup with the Colts, he rushed over to celebrate with the Indianapolis defense whenever it forced a turnover, photobombing as teammates posed for cameras.
“He’s a team-first guy,” said Anthony Walker, a former linebacker who played with Brissett with the Colts and Cleveland Browns. “It was never about, ‘Man, I’m not playing,’ or whatever. It was, ‘I want the team to do well.’ And when that happens, when you’re that selfless of a guy, good things tend to happen to you, right?”
None of this has been easy. As a rookie in 2016, Brissett was one of two quarterbacks who filled in for a suspended Tom Brady after the Deflategate scandal. In Indianapolis, he replaced Luck after Luck unexpectedly retired. In Cleveland, he stepped in after the NFL suspended Deshaun Watson for violating the league’s personal conduct policy. In Arizona, he replaced Kyler Murray, starting the final 12 games of the 2025 season.
This is where Parcells has helped. Brissett has known Parcells since his high school coach introduced them during the quarterback’s time at William T. Dwyer High in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla. Since then, the two have bonded to the point that Brissett no longer considers Parcells a mentor — “like, he’s legit my granddad,” the quarterback said, adding he lives just down the street from Parcells.
His conversations with the former NFL coach have taught him to “never shy from an uncomfortable situation,” Brissett said. It’s easy for backup quarterbacks to try to find a place where it’s easiest to get on the field. Brissett said Parcells pushed him to look at it differently. This may not be the best situation, but it might be good for you . It taught Brissett to try to learn more about himself and see how far he could push.
“He has a pretty good idea of what I think’s important — not that I’m anybody, I’m nobody — but I had a lot of experience in the business and we just got to be friends,” Parcells told The Athletic of their relationship. “I’m very, very proud of him.”
Leadership aside, the biggest knock on Brissett is his record. He is 20-45 as a starter. After he replaced Murray last season, he played well, averaging 280.5 passing yards per game, but the Cardinals went 1-11. At his first news conference of fall camp — after he signed a restructured contract worth $15.5 million that ended a holdout — Brissett was asked whether he had a message for fans about the optics of a quarterback coming off a dismal record asking for more money. Brissett, who had originally signed with Arizona at a rate befitting a backup, said he couldn’t care less — “Deal got done.”
“The wins and losses aren’t a reflection of who I am,” Brissett said when asked about this at the Arizona practice facility. “And (that’s) not just coming from me, but it’s coming from my teammates. I know my value.”
Ron Rivera coached Brissett during the 2023 season with the Washington Commanders. Rivera also interviewed for the Cardinals’ head-coaching position this winter, not long after the organization fired Jonathan Gannon. Before meeting with the Cardinals, Rivera watched film of Arizona’s 2025 season. Had he gotten the job, Rivera said he would have felt comfortable with Brissett at QB1. He liked his poise.
Sometimes, Rivera…

title: AFC North Whiparound: Bengals and Ravens top writers' division-winner predictions Our writers pick division winners, individual award nominees and how they think the four teams will fare this weekend. Paul Dehner Jr., Mike DeFabo and more 39
summary:
Joe Burrow and Lamar Jackson could be facing each for the division title on New Year's Eve. Joseph Maiorana / Imagn Images
Each week during the regular season (and occasionally during the offseason), our AFC North writers tackle the pressing questions and biggest storylines around the division. Today, it’s prediction time. We’re predicting the order of finish, X-factors, award winners and this weekend’s results.
We know the quarterbacks will be the driving force of what happens here, but which n
full_text:
Joe Burrow and Lamar Jackson could be facing each for the division title on New Year's Eve. Joseph Maiorana / Imagn Images
Each week during the regular season (and occasionally during the offseason), our AFC North writers tackle the pressing questions and biggest storylines around the division. Today, it’s prediction time. We’re predicting the order of finish, X-factors, award winners and this weekend’s results.
We know the quarterbacks will be the driving force of what happens here, but which non-quarterback on your team will be the determining factor in whether the team you cover overachieves or underachieves this year?
Mike DeFabo (Steelers): The Aaron Rodgers-Mike McCarthy reunion will be the headline when a new era of Steelers football begins. But for this team to reach its ceiling, new defensive coordinator Patrick Graham will need to get his unit to play up to its paycheck. The new defensive coordinator made a name for himself by doing a lot with a little in Vegas. He now inherits a defense that will be the NFL’s highest-paid for the fifth consecutive season. Graham will bring more coverage disguises to a team that was sometimes predictable. I’m especially interested to see how Graham’s use of simulated pressures could create more one-on-one opportunities for T.J. Watt and company. If you’re looking for a player, Watt is the one with the most pressure on him after two down seasons. Watt needs to play like one of the NFL’s highest-paid non-QBs if this well-compensated defense is going to meet expectations.
Jeff Zrebiec (Baltimore Ravens): For the Ravens to get to where they want to be, Lamar Jackson needs to stay healthy and their defense needs to become formidable again. The key to the latter is Trey Hendrickson. It’s been quite a while since the Ravens had an elite edge rusher, and Hendrickson, assuming he can regain that 2020 to 2024 form, has the ability to transform the defense. Last year’s Ravens couldn’t get to the quarterback, consistently create turnovers or close games. A healthy and motivated Hendrickson should help in all three areas and make the Ravens’ defense better at every level. He’s been especially dangerous in the fourth quarter, where the defense’s inability to get off the field or make a game-changing play has held the team back.
Paul Dehner Jr. (Bengals): Dexter Lawrence. Yeah, the biggest move of the offseason will have the biggest impact on the games, imagine that. But in this case, the variance of outcomes makes it particularly true. Lawrence looks and sounds rejuvenated with his scenery change in Cincinnati. He admitted he’s rediscovered some love of the game and spent the last month wrecking practices. Is he back to being the All-Pro Lawrence from 2022 and 2023? Or will he be closer to the version that played good but not great football on his way out of New York? All aspects of the Bengals’ defensive overhaul depend on Lawrence dominating once again. We’ll see if he does.
Zac Jackson (Browns): New coach Todd Monken. The Browns’ crash continued last year, but ownership doubled down on general manager Andrew Berry and the front office while making a coaching change. Then, Berry traded arguably the NFL’s most dominant player, Myles Garrett, and ownership and Berry endorsed Monken giving Deshaun Watson one more chance. So it’s hard to expect much from this year’s Browns, and the organization seems rightly focused on the future. If Monken creates an offense that’s greatly improved and at least occasionally explosive, maybe the Browns can overachieve. But with a new staff and so many new faces across the coaching staff and offensive roster, even what eventually counts as real growth might be slow.
Over the last three seasons, representatives from the North have won MVP, Defensive Player of the Year, Defensive Rookie of the Year, Comeback Player of the Year and Coach of the Year. What AFC North player would you bet on to win a season-long award in 2026?
DeFabo: Joe Burrow is always in the MVP conversation at this time every year, but the award he’s had to settle for is Comeback Player of the Year. Maybe that changes this season. He’d be a good bet. But for this, I’ll pick his star receiver, Ja’Marr Chase, to win Offensive Player of the Year. He has so much chemistry with Burrow and plenty of other weapons in the offense to free him up.
Zrebiec: Jackson was the unanimous league MVP in his first full year in a Greg Roman-led offense. Jackson finished just one vote shy of his second unanimous league MVP in his first full year in a Todd Monken-led offense. By all accounts, Jackson has fully bought into first-year Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle and that traditionally means dynamic results will follow. Burrow should be in the MVP mix as well and Chase is a perennial candidate for Offensive Player of the Year, but I have to go with a healthy, happy and motivated Jackson.
Dehner Jr.: Hard to pass on Burrow for MVP right now. He’s ranked third by BetMGM (+900) for the award. He’s talking with more confidence and excitement than in any year in recent memory. His story plays right into the voters’ wheelhouse. He’s never won the award despite elite play, held back by team performance or injury. If he puts together a full, healthy season at past levels and the Bengals return to contender status, he’ll be in the MVP conversation all year. The continuity surrounding him and a defense that will have him playing with a touch more caution to keep that interception number low will only bolster what could be a ridiculous touchdown-to-interception ratio on top of the weekly dose of highlight plays he’s created throughout his career.
Jackson: Cleveland’s two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year had to be traded last June. I’m guessing no one is happier about Garrett going to the Rams than Jackson and Burrow are, but the departure likely eliminates the Browns from the NFL’s most significant awards. Speaking of significant, Cleveland rookie wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston are keepers and significant upgrades, but they’d likely have to post outrageous numbers to get rookie of the year consideration. Everything I see says the real award the Browns are chasing is a premium draft pick 230 days from now.
Time to plant your flag: Predict the AFC North order of finish and why.
DeFabo: After a somewhat down year for the division in 2025, I think this will be another season with three AFC North teams in the playoffs. A year ago, everyone was hyping the Ravens as one of the best rosters in football. It seems like this year they’re somewhat under the radar. I have a lot of respect for Jesse Minter and believe he can get the defense to play at a much higher level. As long as he’s healthy, Jackson is still one of the league’s most dynamic players. The Bengals’ improved defensive personnel made me think twice about this pick. I’ll take them second in a tight division race that comes down to the final week. The Steelers will be fighting for a wild-card spot as the third-place finisher in this division, and the Browns will be at the bottom.
Zrebiec: 1. Ravens; 2. Bengals; 3. Steelers; 4. Browns. It’s always foolish to count the Steelers out, and they probably will be playoff-bound again, but for me, it came down to the Ravens versus the Bengals for the top spot. I think both defenses will be dramatically improved, and the two offenses will always be among the league’s best if the quarterbacks stay healthy. I give a slight edge to the Ravens because I think they have the potential to be a little more balanced and I trust their defense more to rebound under a really good defensive head coach. Monken has a ton of fans in Baltimore, and rightly so, but until they have themselves a quarterback, it’s going to be hard to project the Browns to finish outside of last.
Dehner Jr.: 1. Bengals, 2. Ravens, 3. Steelers, 4. Browns. I just tend to believe what I hear, and I hear everyone in the building, specifically Burrow, talking about this team…

full_text:
Highmark Stadium's grass surface came under fire for large divots during the preseason, prompting the Bills to replace the field before their regular-season home opener. Lauren Leigh Bacho / Getty Images
The Buffalo Bills planted new grass at Highmark Stadium 10 months ago. Last week, before playing a real game on it, they ripped out the field and started over.
Before the Bills made this decision, NFL field director Nick Pappas wanted to meet with the Highmark Stadium grounds crew to see the field for himself.
What he saw during the Bills’ Aug. 27 preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers was not only a field that complied with the NFL’s health-and-safety requirements, but also one that left much to be desired when it came to showcasing the best of what the league has to offer. The Bills agreed and decided to re-sod in hopes of fixing a field one of their players called “ass,” and which Pappas said showed “major deformations.”
Why put QB Josh Allen, the league’s MVP favorite, on a substandard playing surface and risk mitigating his greatness, if not his health?
That decision wasn’t up to Pappas, but in an interview with The Athletic , he shared his thoughts on the circumstances Buffalo must navigate in its new $2.2 billion ballpark. A significant test looms with three straight home games in Weeks 2 through 4.
“I have confidence that the staff there will find the best solution for that building,” Pappas said from Australia, where he’ll attend Thursday night’s showcase between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers.
Pappas discussed the challenges of growing grass at Highmark Stadium, teams’ responsibility for field performance, what the NFL will monitor in Buffalo, and whether grass makes sense for every stadium.
What input did the NFL have in the Highmark Stadium field when the team decided to switch to grass after 54 years?
With all of our stadiums, any time there’s discussion around either new stadium construction or, as we’ve seen in the past, the change from one surface to the other, whether that’s grass to artificial or artificial to grass, we work and support our clubs with whatever available, most up-to-date data we have. It’s usually nothing beyond what actually gets shared on a regular basis to our health and safety committees and to our joint surfaces committee.
So, the Bills’ ownership had all the available data, up to date, when making their decisions to build their new stadium and determine the surface type. Beyond that, there was no specific, additional support.
What involvement did the NFL have over the past 10 months at Highmark Stadium?
The league’s involvement with Highmark or any club is ensuring that all fields meet compliance before NFL use, right? So that would be any game day or practice being held inside a stadium or at a practice venue — any NFL field the players are going to be faced with. We ensure compliance is completed. So, there’s a barrage of testing that is mandatory by the NFL and the NFLPA, and that has to happen before players can use the field.
More specifically, beyond that standard compliance, I was present for their final Thursday night preseason game (against the Pittsburgh Steelers) and, obviously, I had some conversations with the Bills leading up to that game, prior to my arrival, just to talk through the conditions and status of their field.
What were those conversations before the preseason finale?
From my perspective, it was just understanding what the Bills’ staff was seeing and experiencing. Obviously, there was attention about the field in the media. Players had made some comments generally about the field. So, it was a conversation to try and get more of an in-person response. The grounds staff was there. Rather than trying to understand what’s happening from what I’m seeing on social media, it was a conversation with the grounds crew just to understand the challenges they may be faced with and the current status and conditions of the playing field.
How did you think the field looked when you saw it firsthand?
I thought it looked great, right? Everybody liked the deep shade of green. But from a playability and compliance perspective, there weren’t any issues. The field met compliance, which is really just a firmness criterion that we have in our mandatory practices. Again, that’s our standards that are created jointly with the NFLPA. I wasn’t surprised that it met compliance because, of course, all our fields would.
The aspect of the field that appeared to be an issue was that there were major deformations happening, large divoting outside of what we typically see at many of our NFL grass fields — although not something we haven’t seen before. That lent itself to say there was an opportunity to improve that surface, and that’s what the Bills have stepped up to do and made that decision to replace it.
What caused the deformations?
I don’t think it’s as cut-and-dry as I would have liked it to be. When I arrived to assess and speak with the grounds crew and try to get a little bit of the last eight, 10 months of historical data since installation, I think you’re dealing with a challenge that I’ve seen happen in the industry anytime there’s a new facility built. There’s a period before it gets turned over to Bills staff. So, you’re now reliant on the general contractor or the installation company for maintenance over a certain period of time. Obviously, a field being installed in a Northern climate in October means that it will likely slow down, if not go dormant, shortly after that, and it will not wake up until after March or April.
So I think it’s a combination of the sod quality from the start, the challenges, and maybe the management up until the Bills’ grounds crew were able to take over, and then you couple it with a very new growing environment that needs to be worked through; it presents challenges. That’s a facility that is going to have lower-light conditions and different airflow. It’s got its own microclimate once you’re inside that building versus standing outside that building. There’s a lot of things that’ll have to be monitored and looked at to determine what’s the best way to manage a playing surface in that building.
How will the first and second fields perform differently?
The new sod being installed will come in thicker than what the existing sod was installed at. In the world of the NFL, that matters. When we talk about grass fields that are being used across the league, the vast majority are Bermuda grass grown on plastic. The concept of growing sod on plastic is one the NFL has really relied on quite heavily to be able to have the level of quality and the ability to turn around and replace a field midseason. It’s growing grass over an impermeable sheet of plastic over a duration of time that would allow it to grow up, grow really thick.
Growing grass in the Northeast presents different challenges because trying to grow bluegrass over an impermeable sheet of plastic when it’s 95 degrees in the summertime is extremely challenging, and you may end up with a product that suffers. Tuckahoe (Turf Farms, which grew Highmark Stadium’s grass) doesn’t currently grow sod on plastic as a bluegrass. They do offer it as a Bermuda grass, but then there are different nuances if you were to introduce Bermuda grass to the Northeast, much like Cleveland, Philadelphia, Chicago and most recently Pittsburgh have done. I don’t think it’s as cut-and-dry as everyone hopes.
The Bills replaced their original field after two preseason games in 13 days. They’re about to play three home games in 18 days. What needs to happen for the new field to work?
They’re going to go forward with their maintenance program. They’ll have a new product, a new field in there, and I suspect it’ll be a vast improvement from the issues that we saw, which was the overall density and strength of the grass. There’s a lot that goes into when their next replacement may be, and it’s likely to happen again, but I say that…

The Carolina Panthers owner forgot or chose not to remember his 2023 NFL Draft night comments about needing fewer “elite receivers” because of Bryce Young’s ability to see the field and distribute the ball like a point guard.
The other not
full_text:
Bryce Young threw for just 154 yards with two interceptions in last season's opener against the Jaguars. Doug Engle / Imagn Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — There were two big takeaways from David Tepper’s media availability this week, his first in nearly three years. The Carolina Panthers owner forgot or chose not to remember his 2023 NFL Draft night comments about needing fewer “elite receivers” because of Bryce Young’s ability to see the field and distribute the ball like a point guard.
The other notable item that emerged from Tepper’s news gathering also involved his quarterback: avoiding the slow starts that have plagued Young and the Panthers the past three seasons.
“We know we can come from behind. We’ve gotta start fast,” Tepper said Wednesday . “We’ve gotta start fast the season. We’ve gotta start fast (in) games. That’s it.”
The Panthers have gone winless in Weeks 1 and 2 every year since 2023, when the Panthers pulled off a big trade with the Chicago Bears to take Young with the No. 1 pick. Young has been awful in those games, posting an NFL-worst 0-6 record (Russell Wilson was next closest at 0-4) and a 64.0 passer rating that is the lowest among 38 qualified passers.
Young has a 58.1 completion percentage in Weeks 1 and 2 (the league average was 65.5 percent in that same span) and a 0.8 touchdown/interception rate (league average 2.0). Those early struggles prompted Frank Reich to give Young a Week 3 reset as a rookie (officially an ankle injury that sources have said Young could have played through) and led Dave Canales to bench Young after two games in 2024.
The Panthers broke a seven-year playoff drought last season and reawakened their fanbase by winning the NFC South and taking the Los Angeles Rams to the wire in a wild-card game at Bank of America Stadium. Entering Sunday’s opener against the Chicago Bears, everyone in the organization — from the owner on down — understands the importance of a strong start to keep the good vibes flowing.
“We’re gonna try not to start slow. Because that feeling of starting slow, like, ‘Ah, s–––, here it goes.’ And it’s not just us. Everybody feels that,” right guard Robert Hunt said. “So hopefully we don’t do that. We’re gonna come out, we’re gonna compete. We’re gonna fly around and hopefully we don’t start that way.”
The Panthers have scored 10 points in each of Young’s three Week 1 starts, falling to the Atlanta Falcons (24-10) in 2023, the New Orleans Saints (47-10) in ’24 and the Jacksonville Jaguars (26-10) last season. Young has thrown two interceptions in each loss, been sacked seven times and finished with a passer rating below 50.0.
“Every year’s a new year. We want to have an emphasis of starting fast. We talked about that a lot as a team, as a unit, as an organization,” Young said. “But we know that comes with work. It’s about just having the best week possible. Going into the game with as much clear communication and being on the same page as we can.”
Young, who reached career highs in every major passing category last year, has been a magician in late-game situations. His 12 game-winning drives in the fourth quarter or overtime are the most in the NFL since 2023, ahead of Patrick Mahomes, Bo Nix and Josh Allen (each with 10). Young trails only Justin Herbert (13) for the most game-winning drives for a quarterback under 25 since 1950.
That’s impressive company. But Tepper suggested the Panthers cannot continue to live on the edge. “We can’t have all come-from-behind wins in the NFL,” he said. “If we get fast starts this year, fast starts to games, we’re gonna win.”
In Young’s first year, when his top receivers were Adam Thielen, D.J. Chark and Jonathan Mingo, the Panthers finished 2-15 and became the only team in NFL history to play a full season without holding a lead in the fourth quarter. (Their two victories came on game-winning field goals by Eddy Pineiro as time expired.)
Since Canales arrived in 2024, the Panthers have been outscored by 221 points in the first half of games, including a whopping 175-point second-quarter differential. They’ve been more competitive in the second half, getting outscored by 56 points.
Canales said the message for Young and the rest of the team is consistency. “What we’ve seen is we can play really great quarters at times. Can we play full games consistently week in and week out?” he said. “And consistency means, hey, if we can play this well down the stretch of a game or we score more points in the second quarter, how about we just be consistent with all of it across the board?
“That includes the first quarter. ‘Guys, we don’t need to wait around to kinda feel it out and see what’s happening. Let’s go get it.’”
To try to get his team out of the gate quicker, Canales asked players to be prepared to rev up the tempo and intensity as soon as they entered the practice fields during training camp. “There can’t be a gradual easing into a practice,” Canales said. “My challenge to the guys was to replicate what it feels like to get your body ready so when you hit the grass, we’re ready to go.”
Wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan said he noticed a difference in the energy in the early portions of practices this summer, but was oblivious to Canales’ intentions until a reporter mentioned it this week. “I didn’t know that’s what he was doing but I definitely felt it, for sure,” he said.
McMillan, last year’s Offensive Rookie of the Year, said the Panthers’ six game-winning drives in 2025 were nice. But there’s a less stressful path to the win column.
“It makes everything hard, not starting the way we wanted to, starting behind the sticks. You never want that,” he said. “But I think based off of last year, we’ve done a good job as far as being behind and coming back. You love to finish games in the fourth quarter, but we wanna make it easy on ourselves by just starting fast.”
Offensive coordinator Brad Idzik, who will make his play-calling debut Sunday, believes maintaining a balanced attack and staying out of second- and third-and-longs can help Young succeed early against the Bears.
“We know he’s special on the edge. We know he’s special on third down and he’s also special outside of the makeshift of the play. He can extend plays. And he does that early (and) often in games. So how do you put him in that mindset?” Idzik said.
“It might not be a perfect set dropback, but it might be moving him off the spot early, getting him in that mindset but complementing it with the run game. Staying ahead of the sticks, that’s really the biggest thing.”
Young’s Week 1 losses have all come on the road. Sunday’s game is the Panthers’ first season opener at BoA Stadium since 2022, when Baker Mayfield started at quarterback in a 26-24 loss to his former Cleveland Browns team.
This week’s matchup features Young and Bears quarterback Caleb Williams, who was drafted No. 1 overall with a pick the Panthers sent to Chicago in that blockbuster trade that brought Young to Charlotte.
But that storyline hasn’t received much play this week. Much of the pregame talk has focused on Young and the Panthers not falling into an early hole — in the game and their season.
“Across the league, if you’re not taking advantage of every snap, every opportunity, every quarter, it’s hard to dig out of deficits at times. Obviously, that’s not something we ever want to do,” Young said.
But Young knows as well as anyone that games don’t always unfold as planned.
“We understand it’s an adversity league. It’s not something you ever want to be accustomed to,” Young said. “But football’s football. It’s part of it. And however things are, we can’t tuck our tail if things don’t go our way at any aspect — start, middle, finish. That’s part of the game and I’m excited for our journey.”

title: How important is it for the Bears to start fast? Mailbag, plus Week 1 picks The Bears want to get off to a hot start, but don't judge the team by how its opening drive goes. Or maybe you should? Kevin Fishbain 6
summary:
Caleb Williams and the Bears scored a touchdown on their first drive of the 2025 season, a rare feat for the franchise. Matt Marton / Imagn Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Every team wants to start hot, but it’s not easy to open an NFL season with a score. The Chicago Bears have done it nine times in the past 25 seasons, one of them last year, when Ben Johnson’s first drive as head coach resulted in a touchdown.
The Bears marched 61 yards in 10 plays in Week 1 of 2025 to take a 7-0 lead on the Viking
full_text:
Caleb Williams and the Bears scored a touchdown on their first drive of the 2025 season, a rare feat for the franchise. Matt Marton / Imagn Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Every team wants to start hot, but it’s not easy to open an NFL season with a score. The Chicago Bears have done it nine times in the past 25 seasons, one of them last year, when Ben Johnson’s first drive as head coach resulted in a touchdown.
The Bears marched 61 yards in 10 plays in Week 1 of 2025 to take a 7-0 lead on the Vikings. No Bears team had opened the season with a touchdown, let alone points, since Matt Nagy’s opening drive in 2018.
In the past 25 seasons, according to Stathead, the opening drive of the Bears’ season has resulted in a touchdown five times, a field goal four times and a punt 14 times. Andy Dalton threw a pick to open the 2021 season against the Los Angeles Rams, and the 2023 Bears turned it over on downs to begin that campaign.
Those nine scores from 2001 to 2025 are tied with the Minnesota Vikings for the most in the NFC North.
“I don’t think there’s any secret to coming out of the gate hot,” Johnson said this week. “I think all 32 teams want to do that right now. Like I said, as a coach a trap that I’ve ran into in the past is trying to bite off a little bit more than you can chew early on in the season. Really our intent as a coaching staff is come out and play fast.”
Johnson was speaking in general about a season opener, but the franchise’s poor starts to seasons piqued my curiosity, especially as they enter this new era of (gasp) the offense being the team’s calling card.
The last time the Bears scored on the opening drive in back-to-back seasons was 2014 to 2016. To illustrate how meaningless that can be, those three teams missed the playoffs. To add to that, the Green Bay Packers, who have had plenty of offensive prowess this century, have had seven season-opening scores and 16 punts out of 25 seasons.
Coaches have months to think about that first script, how the opening drive might look, but it’s never that simple.
Offensive coordinator Press Taylor explained Thursday that during self-scout in organized team activities, the Bears would find things to lean into and other elements of the offense to toss out. But then comes game week and preparation specifically for an opponent.
What if the Bears see something they would do against the Carolina Panthers, but it’s a play they threw out? Then they go back to the drawing board. The key, Taylor said, is making sure they’re playing fast, and they can go to their bread and butter in Week 1 to help that out against unfamiliar defenses.
“We’ve all talked about the unscouted looks that happen early in September football, and how are we gonna handle these, we all got to be on the same page,” he said. “But ultimately we want to be able to find a way to lean into the things we do really well and we’ve done for a really long time so that when things kind of hit the fan and we’re not sure what the defense is or what this personnel grouping is gonna play for us, OK, we’ve run this play a million times and we can find a way to get a completion. We can find a way to get it blocked and get it executed.”
Don’t judge a Bears book by its opening drive. Remember, they didn’t score on their opening drive in any of their final nine games — and they went 6-3 in that stretch. They also scored on the second drive of the game in 10 of 17 weeks.
Then again, five of the Bears’ six division-title seasons this century began with points on the first drive of the season.
Now, on to your questions.
How important is it for this team to start out fast and get a victory in Week 1? We know they bounced back from 0-2 last year, but is that sustainable again this year, given the strength of schedule they are facing and being the hunted, rather than the hunter? — Matt M.
As much as it’d be great for the Bears to start 1-0, I wouldn’t worry about how detrimental a loss would be. Now, if they lose, how they lose would matter more, but weird things can happen in Week 1.
As for the hunted versus the hunter, sure, teams are going to be more aware of the Bears and what Caleb Williams and Johnson can do, but going through media predictions this week, I very rarely saw folks picking the Bears to win the division, let alone advance in the playoffs. As Johnson noted this summer, they are the No. 1 regression candidate, and in a tough division, they’re not really getting a ton of hype outside the city.
With all that said, to your point about the schedule, it would be wise to build up a cushion ahead of a late-season stretch that includes the Buffalo Bills, Packers and Detroit Lions in consecutive weeks.
What does the Bears’ defense have to accomplish this season for you to view it as a “successful unit”? — cardozajack88
In 2025, the Bears ranked No. 21 in defensive expected points added per play, No. 19 against the pass and No. 24 against the run. They were No. 25 in QB hits, No. 21 in sack percentage and No. 29 in pressure percentage. Yet they still won the division and won a playoff game, in large part because of 33 takeaways, which led the league.
What if the defense was purely average? We cannot expect those takeaway numbers to roll over, but can a revamped interior defensive line and the addition of Devin Bush at linebacker help the run defense? Can more comfort in Dennis Allen’s scheme move the defensive EPA up to, say, 16th in the league? Can a healthy Dayo Odeyingbo combined with Austin Booker’s breakout potential move the pass rush to, how about 20th?
Considering the players on the field and those on the injured list (safety Coby Bryant, nickel corner Kyler Gordon), a defense that ranked in the middle of the league as opposed to the bottom third would probably be deemed successful, but it’s all about where the Bears can improve. The woeful run defense and pass rush didn’t prevent them from making a run in the playoffs last season. If this defense can improve on the margins and still be solid in the red zone (15th last season, 10th in goal-to-go situations), it might not require the offense to score 30 per game.
What’s your take on the news that Kyler Gordon is rehabbing away from the Bears with his own trainer? Is this a common practice in the NFL? — AddisonAndClark C.
The disparity between how much attention that news, broken by NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport, received and how much attention I paid to it was vast. After nearly two months of Gordon questions, I’ve kind of reached the point of, wake me up when he’s actually practicing with the team, which can’t happen until after Week 2 at the earliest.
To your question, though, it’s not necessarily uncommon, especially in the offseason. Juxtapose Gordon’s decision, however, with the way general manager Ryan Poles praised Gordon’s decision to stay local during the spring.
“I think he gave up a lot this break to stay here and put the time in,” Poles said in late July.
That seemed to matter to the front office then, but maybe Gordon reached a point with the injury that he had to try something different. Either way, it’s frustrating for everyone involved. Gordon’s performance in the playoff loss to the Rams is a pretty recent reminder of what he can do when healthy. At this point, it’s understandable to speculate about what Gordon could contribute this season and beyond.
In 2027, will Malik Muhammad be listed as a nickel CB or outside CB? — Josh M.
We’re already looking to the future before Muhammad’s NFL debut! But if the Bears do have a long-term starter with their fourth-round pick, it would give them a lot of flexibility. Tyrique Stevenson is in a contract year. Jaylon Johnson will be entering the last year of his deal in 2027. Who knows what Gordon’s status will be.
Muhammad’s future position will be determined, of course, by how he plays in different spots and who’s here next season. He seems in line to start the season as the nickel corner, a big task for a rookie.

title: Can a revamped Bears defensive tackle group find strength in numbers? Dan Wiederer 14
summary:

Over six weeks of his first NFL training camp, Jordan van den Berg decided it would be best if he just dived right in. No dipping a toe in the water to gauge the temperature. No slow descent into the pool either — from ankles, to knees, to waist, to chest.
Nope, the way van den Berg is wired, nothing else
full_text:
Bears defensive tackle Grady Jarrett wasn't at his best last season, but better health and reinforcements around him could make a big difference. Ian Johnson / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
Over six weeks of his first NFL training camp, Jordan van den Berg decided it would be best if he just dived right in. No dipping a toe in the water to gauge the temperature. No slow descent into the pool either — from ankles, to knees, to waist, to chest.
Nope, the way van den Berg is wired, nothing else made sense but a full-launch cannonball and a hope that everyone around him might notice the splash.
Indeed, heads quickly began to turn as the Chicago Bears defensive tackle showed no fear and an abundance of aggressiveness. Through the long mornings at Halas Hall; during joint practices in Cincinnati and Nashville; over 89 snaps of preseason game action, the rookie emerged rather quickly.
“This is a place where you’re able to play with violence and get praise for it,” van den Berg said during the preseason. “I really enjoy that aspect of the game.”
Coaches and teammates have loved seeing that from van den Berg, gushing about the rookie’s rare combination of quickness, power and unrelenting effort.
“He’s explosive. He’s mean. He plays hard,” said defensive line coach Jeremy Garrett.
Grady Jarrett describes van den Berg as “super athletic” and “hungry to work” with “all the ingredients to really continue to develop.”
Added fellow veteran Neville Gallimore: “When you’ve got a kid who plays with a high motor and doesn’t shy away from competition, it’s only going to make the room that much better. … That’s half the battle in being a rookie — just inviting and wanting all the smoke. And then it’s just wanting the opportunity to get better and show the team how much you want it.”
Not to confuse the metaphor here, but van den Berg is after all a genetically blessed 24-year-old — his grandmother an accomplished South African swimmer, grandfather a competitive bodybuilder — who once went viral with his ability to jump out of a pool. All the way from the water back onto the deck in one burst. (Did it, he says, the first time he ever tried that trick, too.)
Now, as van den Berg arrives for his first NFL regular season with Sunday’s Bears-Panthers opener in Charlotte, he is expected to play a sizable role as part of the Bears’ defensive line rotation. And he’s hoping to have an impact for a deep defensive tackle group that boasts a wide variety of talents and experience levels.
Two weeks ago, when general manager Ryan Poles submitted his initial 53-man roster to the NFL office, he did so after trading Gervon Dexter to Atlanta. Back in the early spring, the idea of subtracting a durable 33-game starter (and a former second-round pick) from a defensive line that seemed to be an area of major concern for the Bears would have been unthinkable. But with a series of low-profile additions up front — and intending to bring in players with an attacking mentality and the competitive tenacity coach Ben Johnson desires — Poles quietly upgraded his defensive tackle room in a way that has become arguably one of the deepest, most energized groups in the building.
In April, Poles felt the excitement from his scouting staff about van den Berg and eagerly traded up in Round 6 of the draft to grab him. Before that, he signed a trio of journeymen in free agency — Gallimore on a two-year deal, Kentavius Street and James Lynch on one-year contracts — as veteran reinforcements.
A diamond-in-the-rough find in undrafted free agent Jayden Loving, who spent one season at Wake Forest after two each at Western Kentucky and Bethune-Cookman, has quickly become a win for the Bears, too.
And don’t forget about Grady Jarrett, age 33 and feeling recharged. In his second season with the Bears, Jarrett is suddenly the longest-tenured defensive tackle on the roster and a reliable tone-setter with the way he attacks the craft.
From top to bottom, there’s a lot here to work with. Complementary skill sets. Significant depth. Best of all, perhaps, every player in the mix has the elevated hustle Bears coaches are pushing for and the buy-in to apply what they’re being taught.
Said defensive coordinator Dennis Allen: “We made a concerted effort this offseason that with the guys we brought into the building, you wanted to see their football character come out on tape. You wanted to see guys who played hard and they played physical and they had great effort to the ball.”
During training camp and the preseason, they checked that box.
“I feel really confident with who we have,” Allen said. “With the style we want to play, I think we’ve got guys who can do the things that we want to do.”
To be clear, for Allen’s defense to be as stout as envisioned, the Bears will need Jarrett to be what they paid him to be. In his first season after signing a three-year, $43-million deal in Chicago, he was significantly slowed by a knee injury in the early going. He missed three games in late September and early October and didn’t seem to be his usual spry, disruptive self until the home stretch of the regular season.
Still, it was meaningful that Jarrett stacked some encouraging performances at the end of the regular season and then in the playoffs.
“I took accountability on the final product of what last year was (for me),” he said. “But I’d be mistaken if I didn’t tell you that I was proud of myself with the things I did have to deal with and overcome.
“I’m not the type to really pat myself on the back to go fight the narrative by pulling all the good plays I did have. I just want to go out there and do my best foot forward.”
Still, Jarrett will not be a one-man wrecking crew on the interior this season, which is why the continued jelling of the entire defensive tackle group is vital.
Street figures to start Sunday with Allen impressed by his suddenness off the ball and his fit for the Bears’ style.
“Quite honestly,” Allen said, “I think he was the most productive tackle we had throughout the course of training camp.”
Gallimore’s superpower over six previous NFL seasons has been his motor. And he has felt revived, bringing his competitiveness and passion to a team that wants those qualities to be at the core of its identity.
“My whole career, I’ve taken pride in showing that whatever I have lacked in knowledge, I’d make up for with my effort and how I play the game,” Gallimore said. “Your best resume in football is how hard you play. That’s always been my thing. When you look at the tape, you’ll realize, OK, this guy is going to give you his best for four quarters — or beyond.”
If and when active on game days, Lynch can supply strength and versatility. And Loving has a knack for flipping a switch on the field, transforming quickly from the eager, jovial rookie in the locker room into a powerful and violent man once the ball is snapped.
“The thing that gets you the most excited,” Allen said, “is just how hard he plays. Look, effort is a talent. And he has that.”
Of course, eyes will also continue to lock in on van den Berg, who may have the highest upside of anyone in the defensive tackle room and continues to stimulate the imagination of his coaches, who have seen elite drive and coachability that blend nicely with his athleticism.
At times, van den Berg can find himself getting a little out of control with his play style. He will need to heighten his discipline with what the system is asking from him.
“He’s still learning the game of football to a degree,” Johnson said.
Allen, though, has been impressed with the rookie’s physicality and ability to strike blocks. He is also pushing van den Berg to develop finishing moves, both in how he sheds blocks and makes plays as a run stopper and with how he can eventually become a regular aggravation for opposing quarterbacks.
“A lot of times with defensive linemen, you can have a lot of hidden production where you’re just so disruptive that you create opportunities for other players,”…

title: AFC North Whiparound: Bengals and Ravens top writers' division-winner predictions Our writers pick division winners, individual award nominees and how they think the four teams will fare this weekend. Paul Dehner Jr., Mike DeFabo and more 39
summary:
Joe Burrow and Lamar Jackson could be facing each for the division title on New Year's Eve. Joseph Maiorana / Imagn Images
Each week during the regular season (and occasionally during the offseason), our AFC North writers tackle the pressing questions and biggest storylines around the division. Today, it’s prediction time. We’re predicting the order of finish, X-factors, award winners and this weekend’s results.
We know the quarterbacks will be the driving force of what happens here, but which n
full_text:
Joe Burrow and Lamar Jackson could be facing each for the division title on New Year's Eve. Joseph Maiorana / Imagn Images
Each week during the regular season (and occasionally during the offseason), our AFC North writers tackle the pressing questions and biggest storylines around the division. Today, it’s prediction time. We’re predicting the order of finish, X-factors, award winners and this weekend’s results.
We know the quarterbacks will be the driving force of what happens here, but which non-quarterback on your team will be the determining factor in whether the team you cover overachieves or underachieves this year?
Mike DeFabo (Steelers): The Aaron Rodgers-Mike McCarthy reunion will be the headline when a new era of Steelers football begins. But for this team to reach its ceiling, new defensive coordinator Patrick Graham will need to get his unit to play up to its paycheck. The new defensive coordinator made a name for himself by doing a lot with a little in Vegas. He now inherits a defense that will be the NFL’s highest-paid for the fifth consecutive season. Graham will bring more coverage disguises to a team that was sometimes predictable. I’m especially interested to see how Graham’s use of simulated pressures could create more one-on-one opportunities for T.J. Watt and company. If you’re looking for a player, Watt is the one with the most pressure on him after two down seasons. Watt needs to play like one of the NFL’s highest-paid non-QBs if this well-compensated defense is going to meet expectations.
Jeff Zrebiec (Baltimore Ravens): For the Ravens to get to where they want to be, Lamar Jackson needs to stay healthy and their defense needs to become formidable again. The key to the latter is Trey Hendrickson. It’s been quite a while since the Ravens had an elite edge rusher, and Hendrickson, assuming he can regain that 2020 to 2024 form, has the ability to transform the defense. Last year’s Ravens couldn’t get to the quarterback, consistently create turnovers or close games. A healthy and motivated Hendrickson should help in all three areas and make the Ravens’ defense better at every level. He’s been especially dangerous in the fourth quarter, where the defense’s inability to get off the field or make a game-changing play has held the team back.
Paul Dehner Jr. (Bengals): Dexter Lawrence. Yeah, the biggest move of the offseason will have the biggest impact on the games, imagine that. But in this case, the variance of outcomes makes it particularly true. Lawrence looks and sounds rejuvenated with his scenery change in Cincinnati. He admitted he’s rediscovered some love of the game and spent the last month wrecking practices. Is he back to being the All-Pro Lawrence from 2022 and 2023? Or will he be closer to the version that played good but not great football on his way out of New York? All aspects of the Bengals’ defensive overhaul depend on Lawrence dominating once again. We’ll see if he does.
Zac Jackson (Browns): New coach Todd Monken. The Browns’ crash continued last year, but ownership doubled down on general manager Andrew Berry and the front office while making a coaching change. Then, Berry traded arguably the NFL’s most dominant player, Myles Garrett, and ownership and Berry endorsed Monken giving Deshaun Watson one more chance. So it’s hard to expect much from this year’s Browns, and the organization seems rightly focused on the future. If Monken creates an offense that’s greatly improved and at least occasionally explosive, maybe the Browns can overachieve. But with a new staff and so many new faces across the coaching staff and offensive roster, even what eventually counts as real growth might be slow.
Over the last three seasons, representatives from the North have won MVP, Defensive Player of the Year, Defensive Rookie of the Year, Comeback Player of the Year and Coach of the Year. What AFC North player would you bet on to win a season-long award in 2026?
DeFabo: Joe Burrow is always in the MVP conversation at this time every year, but the award he’s had to settle for is Comeback Player of the Year. Maybe that changes this season. He’d be a good bet. But for this, I’ll pick his star receiver, Ja’Marr Chase, to win Offensive Player of the Year. He has so much chemistry with Burrow and plenty of other weapons in the offense to free him up.
Zrebiec: Jackson was the unanimous league MVP in his first full year in a Greg Roman-led offense. Jackson finished just one vote shy of his second unanimous league MVP in his first full year in a Todd Monken-led offense. By all accounts, Jackson has fully bought into first-year Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle and that traditionally means dynamic results will follow. Burrow should be in the MVP mix as well and Chase is a perennial candidate for Offensive Player of the Year, but I have to go with a healthy, happy and motivated Jackson.
Dehner Jr.: Hard to pass on Burrow for MVP right now. He’s ranked third by BetMGM (+900) for the award. He’s talking with more confidence and excitement than in any year in recent memory. His story plays right into the voters’ wheelhouse. He’s never won the award despite elite play, held back by team performance or injury. If he puts together a full, healthy season at past levels and the Bengals return to contender status, he’ll be in the MVP conversation all year. The continuity surrounding him and a defense that will have him playing with a touch more caution to keep that interception number low will only bolster what could be a ridiculous touchdown-to-interception ratio on top of the weekly dose of highlight plays he’s created throughout his career.
Jackson: Cleveland’s two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year had to be traded last June. I’m guessing no one is happier about Garrett going to the Rams than Jackson and Burrow are, but the departure likely eliminates the Browns from the NFL’s most significant awards. Speaking of significant, Cleveland rookie wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston are keepers and significant upgrades, but they’d likely have to post outrageous numbers to get rookie of the year consideration. Everything I see says the real award the Browns are chasing is a premium draft pick 230 days from now.
Time to plant your flag: Predict the AFC North order of finish and why.
DeFabo: After a somewhat down year for the division in 2025, I think this will be another season with three AFC North teams in the playoffs. A year ago, everyone was hyping the Ravens as one of the best rosters in football. It seems like this year they’re somewhat under the radar. I have a lot of respect for Jesse Minter and believe he can get the defense to play at a much higher level. As long as he’s healthy, Jackson is still one of the league’s most dynamic players. The Bengals’ improved defensive personnel made me think twice about this pick. I’ll take them second in a tight division race that comes down to the final week. The Steelers will be fighting for a wild-card spot as the third-place finisher in this division, and the Browns will be at the bottom.
Zrebiec: 1. Ravens; 2. Bengals; 3. Steelers; 4. Browns. It’s always foolish to count the Steelers out, and they probably will be playoff-bound again, but for me, it came down to the Ravens versus the Bengals for the top spot. I think both defenses will be dramatically improved, and the two offenses will always be among the league’s best if the quarterbacks stay healthy. I give a slight edge to the Ravens because I think they have the potential to be a little more balanced and I trust their defense more to rebound under a really good defensive head coach. Monken has a ton of fans in Baltimore, and rightly so, but until they have themselves a quarterback, it’s going to be hard to project the Browns to finish outside of last.
Dehner Jr.: 1. Bengals, 2. Ravens, 3. Steelers, 4. Browns. I just tend to believe what I hear, and I hear everyone in the building, specifically Burrow, talking about this team…

title: People, process, perspective: How Jack Campbell proved the Lions right Campbell cares deeply, especially about the people who were there in the early stages of this journey to the NFL. Colton Pouncy 15
summary:
Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell (Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; Photos: David Reginek / Imagn Images, Gregory Shamus / Getty Images)
DETROIT — Out of uniform and out of his comfort zone, about a week before the chaos ensues, Jack Campbell could, and probably should, be doing just anything else with his time.
With his season around the corner and so few days off remaining, it’s understandable to suggest as much. And yet, his black Ford pickup truck pulls into a parking lo
full_text:
Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell (Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; Photos: David Reginek / Imagn Images, Gregory Shamus / Getty Images)
DETROIT — Out of uniform and out of his comfort zone, about a week before the chaos ensues, Jack Campbell could, and probably should, be doing just anything else with his time.
With his season around the corner and so few days off remaining, it’s understandable to suggest as much. And yet, his black Ford pickup truck pulls into a parking lot in Metro Detroit at the agreed-upon time of 8 a.m. ET on the first Saturday of September. Out hops Campbell to greet the reporter standing before him and settle in for a 90-minute conversation on a subject that, if it were up to him, he’d never have to discuss.
“I don’t know why I get uncomfortable when the focus is me,” Campbell says during our interview.
It’s no secret that talking to media is, um, lower on the list of job perks for Campbell. But fresh off the most transformative season of the All-Pro linebacker’s career, the focus on him has never been greater. So when a story to discuss it all was pitched to him in January, hoping to discuss the year that was, Campbell agreed and made good on his word. It’s what he does.
You see, Campbell is, in fact, a people person. Just not in the traditional sense. His rough exterior and no-nonsense approach tend to typecast him as a football machine devoid of personality or emotion. Some of it is of his own volition.
When Campbell was a rookie in 2023, a smile from him was so rare that his then-position coach Kelvin Sheppard had to ask if he enjoys this life. “ Shepp, it ain’t you,” Sam LaPorta, Campbell’s college roommate and now NFL teammate, would tell him . “He’s been like that.” During a joint practice that year with the Jacksonville Jaguars, Campbell accidentally took down running back JaMycal Hasty in a non-padded practice. He claims Hasty tripped, but that didn’t stop Jaguars players from leaving the sideline to approach Campbell about it. The rookie was unfazed. “ I mean, I’ll stand on the sideline and face whoever,” Campbell said after practice . “I mean, I don’t really care.”
The following year, after a physical practice against the New York Giants in which several fights broke out, Campbell’s right glove was soaked in blood after a tackle attempt. “ I’ve had tougher practices at Iowa,” Campbell said with a straight face. And against the Baltimore Ravens last September, Campbell took a cleat to the mouth in an act of friendly fire, gushing blood for the rest of the game. He continued to call the defense, as a Joker-like laceration formed across his mouth that later required stitches. “ He’s at the end of the game trying to call plays, and blood’s spitting out everywhere ,” Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said. Jack didn’t get what all the fuss was about.
“ People try to make it seem like it’s super tough,” he said. “… All you gotta do is be able to breathe .”
These are vignettes of the tone-setter the Lions drafted Campbell to be. Just don’t mistake his stoicism for apathy.
He cares. Deeply. Not so much about the people who thought the Lions reached to select him with the 18th pick in the 2023 draft. He has thoughts on them. We’ll get to that later.
Rather, Campbell cares about the people who were there in the early stages of this journey. About the people who molded him along the way. About the people who’ve invested in him long enough to have seen the returns. About the people in Michigan who support him and his team each Sunday, and the people he’ll spend his Sundays with decades from now — when it’s all said and done.
Spend some time with the man behind the helmet, and he’ll tell you what this is all about.
Ask Campbell about his hometown of Cedar Falls, Iowa, and he’ll tell you about the relationships he built there.
He begins by thanking his immediate and extended family, for the sacrifices they made and the way he was raised. He takes a moment to shout out his best friends from back home, retracing steps in his mind, hoping not to leave anyone out. They know who they are.
It’s the people who make it special.
“It’s not a town where everyone knows everyone because it’s so big,” Campbell says, “but I would say it’s a town where if you were ever in need of help, people would lend a hand.”
You can see this instilled in Campbell, both then and now. In high school, Campbell befriended a student named Will Reinart. A fellow Cedar Falls native, Reinart was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia when he was 9 years old. Years of chemotherapy. A stroke that forced him to miss time and school and even relearn how to walk.
Building friendships was sometimes difficult for Reinart, given the circumstances. It wasn’t with Campbell.
A budding linebacker at Cedar Falls High, Campbell heard Reinart’s story and offered his support. He’d carry Reinart’s books to class, walk with him in the hall, talk sports with him; he even helped the school raise money for a Coaches Against Cancer fundraiser. Reinart, in turn, gave Campbell a bracelet that read, “WILL POWER,” with the Bible verse John 3:16.
Campbell wore it every day. All the way to the NFL.
In 2019, Campbell and Reinart were set to graduate. Campbell walked with the rest of his classmates, but Reinart had to miss the ceremony. A school counselor planned a mini-graduation just for Reinart and enlisted Campbell to help spread the word to students. They held it in the high school’s auditorium. Members of the band played “Pomp and Circumstance,” as Reinart took the stage in his red graduation gown and a walker. A turnout of a few dozen would’ve sufficed. A few hundred came.
“He worked his whole life to get to walk across the stage, and then he wasn’t able to with everybody,” Campbell recalled. “Getting to be there, and see that the kids in your grade care enough to come and pay respect to the journey and the battle that he went through to get to walk across that stage, … it’s something that I’ll honestly never forget.”
During the 2019 season, his first at Iowa, Campbell stayed in touch with Reinart, who was studying biology at Hawkeye Community College and hoped to become a physician. Before or after a game, he’d check his phone and could typically find an endearing message from Reinart — an Iowa superfan who now got to root for a close friend. Campbell was primarily a special teams contributor back then, but those words of encouragement meant the world to him as he navigated life in the Big Ten.
One day, those messages stopped. In January 2020, Reinart died. A devastating loss for the community.
Campbell was a pallbearer at Will’s funeral, at the request of Reinart’s family.
“From my perspective, Jack took Will under his wing,” Susan Reinart, Will’s mother, told Hawkeye Headquarters years ago . “He’s just a down-to-earth kid who has a big heart and cares about people, and uses his talent to help others.”
“I was just trying to be there to have a genuine friendship with him and let him know that I’m there for him,” Campbell said. “… To get to be a pallbearer in his funeral was just a huge honor, and something I’ll never forget. The lessons that I learned from Will and everything that went down throughout that time period, I hold with me throughout my daily life.”
All he had to do was look to his wrist for a reminder. It served him well at Iowa.
Kirk Ferentz once said if he had five Jack Campbells, they’d be his three starting linebackers and two starting defensive ends.
“I don’t know if the defensive ends are gonna be eating too much on third downs,” Campbell said, flashing his self-deprecating sense of humor. “But I appreciate that Coach believes in me that much.”
Campbell can laugh about it these days, but there was a time when he wasn’t sure if he’d ever play meaningful snaps at Iowa. Many top high school recruits these days commit to schools expecting to start as true freshmen and hit the league in three years. Campbell was realistic.
He understood there was…

full_text:
MarShawn Lloyd, right, and receiver Matthew Golden, left, celebrate a touchdown during their preseason game against the Broncos. Ron Chenoy / Imagn Images
GREEN BAY, Wis. — If you’re skeptical about the Green Bay Packers this season, you’re not alone.
The Packers have tremendous talent and can be a legitimate Super Bowl contender. The likes of quarterback Jordan Love, tight end Tucker Kraft, edge rusher Micah Parsons and safety Xavier McKinney are among the league’s best at their positions.
They have what should be great wide receiver and linebacker rooms, specifically at the top of those depth charts with Edgerrin Cooper, Zaire Franklin, Christian Watson, Jayden Reed and Matthew Golden. They have promise on both the offensive and defensive lines. They have enticing young players at running back in MarShawn Lloyd and cornerback in rookie second-rounder Brandon Cisse.
For me, though, there are far too many questions about the 2026 Packers to feel confident they can be any different than what they’ve been the last three seasons: a good team, not a great one, that makes the playoffs but exits quickly.
At quarterback, can Tyrod Taylor provide the same jolt Malik Willis did if Love misses time? The answer is probably no.
Major questions loom over Josh Jacobs as the running back awaits a possible NFL suspension resulting from a battery incident in May. He pleaded no contest to the misdemeanor charges. Can Lloyd be a worthwhile No. 1 back in Jacobs’ absence and handle a big workload after playing one game in his first two years? Are Chris Brooks and Kaleb Johnson good enough to keep that room afloat in a by-committee approach?
You feel pretty good about the wide receiver and tight end rooms, but the offensive line is in a precarious position days from the season opener. Is Jordan Morgan any good at left tackle? Can Aaron Banks and Zach Bako-Bewele keep their knees healthy? How will Jacob Monk play at a new starting spot?
On the edge, Lukas Van Ness will finally need to show why he was a first-round pick and others must pick up the slack if Parsons misses the first five games.
At cornerback, will Keisean Nixon play like he did in the first half of last season (good) or the second (not good)? It remains to be seen whether Cisse is the de facto No. 1 corner because he’s that good or because the guys behind him are so underwhelming.
Oh, and it wouldn’t be a series of Packers questions without one about special teams. Will the third time be the charm for a rookie kicker in the post-Mason Crosby era? Trey Smack was perfect in preseason games, but the pressure turns up when the real games start.
How about the head coach who signed an extension after a third consecutive No. 7 seed? Matt LaFleur needs to rally the troops to finish games stronger, hold onto big leads and finally get over the hump.
The Packers don’t need positive answers to all those questions to contend for a title. Heck, they were 9-3-1, atop the division and holding the NFC’s No. 2 seed entering Week 15 last season. They had been without Kraft, perhaps the league’s best tight end, for five weeks. Jacobs was playing hurt, Watson and Reed missed extended stretches with injuries, Van Ness was injured, Rashan Gary was fading and Nixon wasn’t the same player as in the season’s first half. It was only after that day in Denver, when Parsons tore his ACL, Bako-Bewele partially tore his patellar tendon and Watson went to the hospital to rule out dislocated ribs (he ended up playing the next game), that Green Bay’s season crumbled.
The Packers just can’t have that avalanche hit them again, and they need guys such as Morgan and Van Ness to turn those question marks into exclamation points.
Just because I’m skeptical doesn’t mean I’m out on the Packers. That’s hardly the case. My skepticism could morph into optimism by 6:30 p.m. CT on Sunday in Minneapolis, and maybe that’s a me problem for being too reactionary to a Week 1 game.
Van Ness might have two sacks, Morgan might keep his quarterback spotless, Lloyd might run 15 times for 100 yards and two touchdowns and Nixon might limit Justin Jefferson to five catches for 58 yards. I just can’t say with authority yet that I think all those things will happen to make me feel differently about this team in the long run. Not based on what I’ve seen in past seasons and certainly not based on what I’ve seen in makeshift football on Ray Nitschke Field this summer. And even if they do happen, I’ll probably return to Earth by Monday morning and say I need to see the same for a couple more weeks to truly believe in the Packers’ future prospects.
It certainly helps that the Packers get their best player back in Week 5 or 6 — at least that’s what it seems right now — but they have to get there with their head above water. Doing so will require several of those aforementioned guys to perhaps exceed expectations against an albeit underwhelming schedule to start the season. The Packers visit the Minnesota Vikings and New York Jets before hosting the Atlanta Falcons, visiting the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and hosting the Chicago Bears in Week 5.
Let’s say Parsons returns against his old team in Week 6. If the Packers go 5-0 or 4-1 before he returns, brilliant. If they go 3-2, fine. If they go 2-3, not a disaster, but there are probably other issues that need fixing, even with Parsons back to make a playoff push. If they stumble into Week 6 at 1-4 or 0-5, sound the alarm.
This is my eighth season covering the Packers, and except for the lead-up to Love’s first season starting, I can’t remember another in LaFleur’s tenure with this much uncertainty. That season featured a new starting quarterback and the league’s youngest team, with few expectations to go far. That’s how you were supposed to feel then.
This season features a roster constructed to go all in. There’s no house money anymore. They’re still relatively young, but that’s not an excuse with this much big-game experience. It’s win now or continue to disappoint. The Packers haven’t gone this long without an NFC North title since the division became its current form in 2002. They haven’t reached the Super Bowl in more than 15 years. Who knows what the stipulations in LaFleur’s new contract are regarding team success as it relates to his job security, but there’s still pressure to perform for everyone inside 1265 Lombardi Ave., even if there’s no hot-seat talk for the head coach.
Watching this team regularly, I’m not sure it can deliver under pressure and answer all those questions affirmatively. I have to see it to believe it.

title: The Texans defense could become legendary. How they'll do it is their real magic The Texans' defense is different. Players know it. They also know what they want to become next. Jourdan Rodrigue 4

Coach DeMeco Ryans, pass rusher Will Anderson Jr., defensive coordinator Matt Burke, cornerback Kamari Lassiter and safety Jalen Pitre are among the pillars of a Houston Texans defense that thrives on coordination and control. Illustration: Dan Goldfarb / The Athletic; Cooper Neill, Michael Owens, Scott Winters / Getty, Joe Robbins / AP, USA Today
