full_text:
Coach DeMeco Ryans, pass rusher Will Anderson Jr., defensive coordinator Matt Burke, cornerback Kamari Lassiter and safety Jalen Pitre are among the pillars of a Houston Texans defense that thrives on coordination and control. Illustration: Dan Goldfarb / The Athletic; Cooper Neill, Michael Owens, Scott Winters / Getty, Joe Robbins / AP, USA Today
It was August in Houston, and the air was so hot and dense and still that it pressed against the lively talk throughout the Texans’ defense, shaping their language into secrets only they know.
Coordinator Matt Burke, the defensive signal caller, took his spot along the sideline. Behind his graying beard, his expression crackled between a scowl and a mad grin. Players’ jerseys and pads were soaked with sweat. Droplets of it scattered across the grass like shiny little seeds with their movements. Head coach DeMeco Ryans stood calmly near one end zone, monitoring. Every player and coach seemed aware of where he was, and he of them.
The Raiders were in town for a joint practice. Per the two teams’ rules of engagement — and the NFL’s own — the players couldn’t fully tackle each other but instead had to execute what is called “thud”-tackling, meaning some contact is allowed but not the punishing, rip-to-the-earth physicality the Texans defense has become known for.
But removing full force only revealed more intricate, exceptional details of a defense that combines power and control like few can. Houston practiced at full speed, yet to a player the defenders had such mastery over their bodies and thus their impact that it felt like some sort of sleight-of-hand trick as to where the leftover kinetic energy disappeared. Their defensive linemen, captained by star edge rusher Will Anderson Jr., exploded off the line of scrimmage and visibly stressed out both Las Vegas quarterback Kirk Cousins, a veteran, and the rookie No. 1 pick, Fernando Mendoza. Versatile slot defender Jalen Pitre circled formations and dove into plays like a hornet, at one point escorting a larger ball carrier to the sideline and out of bounds in a manner that looked genuinely polite, even as it was clear that the player was helpless to redirect. Even as Texans players thud-tackled, more than once a defender flipped his body at contact and released his opponent so he, not they, would tumble to the grass.
It wasn’t just that the talent differential was so stark between the Texans, a Super Bowl contender , and the rebuilding Raiders; it was the way they handled the practice. It was downright professional, and nearly unexplainable. How can people that size move like that by themselves, let alone in concert?
They are different. They know it. And after the Texans’ defense spent an offseason following a nearly perfect year studying, nitpicking and speaking to what they are, they also know what they want to become next.
In a defensive meeting during training camp, Burke retold a story that was told by British explorer Louis Rudd, the second person to ski solo across Antarctica.
Rudd explained that he always took 11 extra steps at the end of each travel day in honor of the infamous Terra Nova expedition — in which one of two groups competing to arrive at the South Pole not only fell short of the other by 34 days, but also tragically perished on the return journey just 11 miles from an outpost that could have saved them. Rudd said the 11 steps represented a calculation often discussed among voyagers: that with just 11 extra steps per day, that historic travel party may have reached its destination.
“Can we take these next 11 (steps)?” Burke said. “Can you watch one more clip? Can you take two extra minutes to figure something out? Can you ask a question? Whatever those 11 steps are, can you not go to bed at the end of the day without making sure you take those steps? You don’t know (what it will lead to). But can you ensure that you’re not short (of what) is there?”
Burke, who has been Houston’s defensive coordinator since 2023, is a long-distance hiker and mountain climber in his off time. He has summited Mount Kilimanjaro and the Grand Teton, including true rock climbing areas where he had to be roped into part of his ascent and rappel for part of his descent. He has climbed 20,000 feet up Mount Everest; he once backpacked through the Gobi Desert.
“I like being out in the vastness of things,” he said. “And then there’s the goal achievement.”
Burke doesn’t hike specifically to come up with motivational ideas for his players, but he brings some back to them anyway. After Kilimanjaro, he told players what it felt like to see a false peak.
“We made the playoffs the last three years. … Won the first game, then lost in the divisional round,” he said. “I’m like, ‘hey man, there’s this false summit. You’re summiting Kilimanjaro, and all you see is the rim of the crater. … You get up there and you think it’s over. … You still have to hike the f—ing rest of the rim and up the actual summit. It’s a mindf—.
“So, we’ve hit this false summit before. What are we doing (next)?”
The Texans defense is very clear on what it is and how it will attack. That is the key word: They run an attacking defensive front, which means they do not acquiesce to what an offense is trying to get them to read in a play.
“We want to dictate. Defenses, by nature, are reactionary,” Burke said. “The way we play our front is an attempt to be a little more proactive, be on the front foot. You have to react to what we’re doing. We’re not reading blocks. We’re getting off (the line of scrimmage), and you better be ready for us.”
Typically, a high-level compliment for a secondary is that it plays “on a line,” meaning each player’s movements correspond to another in a constant ripple effect. But in Houston, that extends to the inside linebackers, flows inward to the defensive tackles and rolls outward to the edge rushers, too. Pitre switches to a linebacker role in run support and can still cover bigger players from the slot, but the cornerbacks can swing down to tackle, too, if an offense tries to divert its plays away from the defensive line. They can transform their various coverages around their front in an instant, and at game speed — playing slightly varying shades of a coverage an opponent thinks it has studied, but that suddenly feels different.
“The things that we adjust and (when we) tweak rules, ‘can we buy a little bit of a tick (of hesitation)’? Maybe you think it’s quarters, but it’s not quite the same quarters that you saw on tape last week,” Burke said. “When you figure it out, Will Anderson has won his (pass rush). … Or do we get a little indecisiveness, (the quarterback) takes the checkdown and then you’re just there to tackle.”
They are emotionally connected, smart, fast and physical. They show who they are by how they play. Kamari Lassiter, a starting cornerback, itches so badly to get into the run game that sometimes it looks as if an outside force is magnetically pulling him to the action. Pitre, a team captain, is equal parts emotion and control — a player who “completely gives of himself” to the game, said Burke. “He exposes his soul.” Anderson Jr. is the thermostat. Players and coaches say, “however Will decides a practice will go, that’s how it will go.”
Their common language is perfectionism. Each player on the Texans defense is so detailed, so specific in how he can communicate his role that sometimes Ryans has them lead team meetings and film study.
In last year’s ugly divisional round loss to New England, Houston’s offense gained just 241 yards and turned the ball over five times, including four interceptions (one returned for a touchdown). Coaches remember Lassiter voicing his displeasure afterward — with himself. He had been targeted eight times by Patriots quarterback Drake Maye, breaking up three passes and only allowing two catches for 27 yards. To a typical observer, the Texans’ offense lost the game. But Lassiter was angry with himself for not impacting it more…

full_text:
Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor hasn't been to the playoffs since his rookie season. Mykal McEldowney / Imagn Images
Jonathan Taylor is in rarefied air. The Indianapolis Colts running back is already the franchise leader in rushing touchdowns, and he’s just one more dominant, yet doable, season from surpassing Hall of Famer Edgerrin James as the team’s all-time leading rusher. Taylor said Thursday he wasn’t sure how many yards he needed to claim the top spot — it’s 1,629 — but he is aware of something that’s haunted him: the Colts’ playoff drought.
Indianapolis’ last postseason appearance was during Taylor’s rookie season in 2020. After that, he thought trips to the playoffs would be a yearly routine. But every season since has been filled with heartbreak and disappointment, as the Colts have fallen short.
“I can’t wait to get back there,” Taylor said just days before the Colts host the Baltimore Ravens in their season opener.
But will they get back there?
I’ve shared my thoughts several times this offseason on how I think this Colts campaign will unfold, and I’ll give one more season prediction before Sunday. But before I look into the future, I wanted you all to look, as well. As always, I appreciate the Colts fans who were willing to answer one simple but big question: What will happen in 2026? Here are three predictions that stood out.
(Editor’s note: Questions have been edited for clarity.)
I have them at 12-5. Quarterback Daniel Jones will miss a couple of games, but Anthony Richardson Sr. will go .500 in his two starts. Taylor will not tail off the last third of the season as in prior years, and he’ll be a candidate for NFL Offensive Player of the Year. One of the rookie defenders will be a revelation and a future star. Laiatu Latu will have double-digit sacks. The Colts will win the division and a playoff game. — Ray B.
This was, by far, the most optimistic response I received. Twelve wins would be the most the Colts have recorded in a regular season since 2009, which was the last time they reached the Super Bowl (with some guy named Peyton Manning). A prediction this bold suggests Ray B. believes last year’s 8-2 start was no fluke, but I’m not sure I’m as confident, particularly because of Jones’ injury history. I do think, however, Jones is capable of playing good football again, and if Richardson has to step in for a couple of games, that wouldn’t be the worst scenario.
Richardson, the No. 4 pick in the 2023 draft, didn’t pan out as the face of the franchise, but he’s still one of the better backups in the league. Couple that with a breakout campaign from Latu, steady play from rookie Day 2 draft picks CJ Allen and A.J. Haulcy and another strong season from Taylor, then I can squint my eyes and see an AFC South title — Indy’s first since 2014 — and perhaps a playoff victory. In that case, I think it’s safe to say general manager Chris Ballard and coach Shane Steichen, who should both be on the hot seat in 2026, would be retained.
The Colts go 9-8, 5-1 to end the season, and earn a wild-card berth. Jones finishes second to Patrick Mahomes in NFL Comeback Player of the Year voting. Big years from wide receivers Josh Downs and Alec Pierce. Taylor and tight end Tyler Warren basically repeat their 2025 stats. But the pass rush holds the defense back. Steichen gets extended, and I’m worried that means Ballard is back, too. — Paul (@HoosierInMN)
Since Paul has the Colts going 5-1 over their final six games, that means they’d start 4-7 and have to dig themselves out of a hole. I do think Indy’s schedule is a bit easier, at least on paper, at the end of the year than at the beginning, though I’m not sure if this team can be trusted to win late-season games. Amid the Colts’ five-year playoff drought, which is tied for the third-longest active drought in the NFL, they have a 9-17 record in December and January. If Jones and company can buck that trend, then Jones would absolutely be in contention for NFL Comeback Player of the Year.
Aside from the offense, I think Paul’s right to be skeptical about the defense, specifically Indy’s edge rushers. Latu may take a leap in 2026, but I’m not sure that will be enough to offset the other side of the D-line, where the Colts plan to use a defensive end-by-committee approach. If they are somehow able to overcome that roster deficiency and reach the postseason, it wouldn’t shock me if Ballard, who is entering the last year of his contract, lands a new deal to stay tethered to Steichen, who is under contract through 2028. But it also wouldn’t shock me if Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon still moved on. Keep in mind, she has repeatedly stated this offseason that “the sense of urgency has never been higher” for the franchise, and I’m not sure if a wild-card appearance is enough to justify running it back with Ballard.
Indy finishes 7-10; Jones lasts 10 games due to injury, and other injuries reveal the lack of playable depth on the offensive line. The D-line is also mediocre. — Jhan C.
There’s not a lot of sunshine in this succinct prediction, but I’m not mad at the reasoning. Injuries are a huge part of football, and as Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner noted Thursday, every team that goes on a deep playoff run typically has good overall health. The problem with Jones, who’s made a remarkable comeback from his torn right Achilles, is that he’s played only one full season through his first seven. Fittingly, the last time Jones made it to the finish line was when he steered the New York Giants to the playoffs in 2022. But if he’s sidelined again for an extended period in 2026, and Indy’s starting O-line becomes hobbled as well, I agree things could get ugly.
The Colts’ backup offensive linemen don’t have much in-game experience to rely on, and as we discussed, their D-line, particularly on the edge, leaves a lot to be desired. In this seven-win scenario, I think a backslide of that magnitude would result in Ballard and Steichen being relieved of their duties as the Colts explore a long-term rebuild.
I appreciate the variety of responses I received, so now it’s time for me to weigh in, too. In my final prediction for the 2026 season, I think the Colts will finish 10-7 and reach the playoffs for the first time since 2020. They won’t win the division, however, and will lose in the wild-card round. Maybe I’m being overzealous about Jones’ Achilles recovery, but if he stays healthy — which is a big if — I’m convinced he can once again play at a Pro Bowl-caliber level under Steichen’s tutelage and with a skill position group that now features six-time Pro Bowler Keenan Allen.
“I feel like we’ve built good chemistry already through practice,” Jones said of Allen on Wednesday. “… He’s a really experienced, smart football player, so there’s things he sees and understands that you don’t have to explain or go through and talk about every single little situation. There are things that he does naturally from playing for so many years and (he’s) just a really high-IQ football player.”
The defense, however, does give me pause. I think the Colts’ pass rush (or lack thereof) and linebacker group can be exploited, so I’m curious to see how defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo will try to offset some of those weaknesses with his game plans. But regardless of how creative Anarumo gets, I’m not convinced the Colts’ defense will be good enough to hold up for a deep playoff run.
If the Colts do indeed get bounced in the opening round of the postseason, it’ll be interesting to see if a playoff berth is enough success for Ballard to keep his job, or if Indy will finally part ways with one of the longest-tenured GMs in the AFC. The answers will be revealed in the coming months, starting Sunday at Lucas Oil Stadium.

full_text:
Chiefs rookie offensive tackle Khalil Benson, left, will make his NFL debut under the bright lights of "Monday Night Football." Mike Carlson / Getty Images
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — Kansas City Chiefs assistant general manager Mike Bradway would love for the team to take full credit for finding a hidden gem in undrafted rookie offensive tackle Kahlil Benson.
His conscience won’t let him, though.
“There’s certainly, in this case,” Bradway told The Athletic on Aug. 12, “probably some luck involved.”
Here’s the truth: The Chiefs didn’t select Benson during the seven rounds of April’s NFL Draft. And even afterward, they didn’t appear to need another offensive tackle on their 90-man roster.
Benson had been on the team’s draft board, yes. But when pro scout and player personnel coordinator Madison Aponte called Benson’s agent about the possibility of Benson showing up to the team’s rookie minicamp, it was mostly about adding practice bodies while giving Benson a brief chance to prove he belonged.
What’s happened since has become one of the NFL’s great preseason underdog stories — and could be one of the Chiefs’ greatest long-shot tales ever.
Not only did the Chiefs sign Benson after he stood out among 100 players at rookie minicamp in May. But he’s also progressed up the depth chart and is now the team’s expected starter at left tackle for Week 1 against the Denver Broncos, with starter Josh Simmons sidelined because of a back injury.
“He’s obviously shown us that he has ability to play,” coach Andy Reid said of Benson on Thursday. “We wouldn’t put him in there if we didn’t think that.”
It stands to be a historic feat. Per TruMedia, Reid never started an undrafted rookie in Week 1 during his first 13 seasons with the team. The Chiefs’ only undrafted rookie since 2000 to start in Week 1, meanwhile, was fullback Mike Cox in 2008.
If anything, it only speaks to Benson’s extraordinary rise — and also to the Chiefs’ faith in him to perform in an unfamiliar place.
Reid hinted this week that the plan would be to put Benson at left tackle and veteran Jaylon Moore at right. That’s noteworthy because in Benson’s entire college career at Indiana and Colorado, he primarily played left and right guard and right tackle.
The number of college snaps he took at left tackle? Zero.
Moore, the team’s expected starter at right tackle, said working with Benson over the last few months gave him confidence in how the rookie will perform Monday night. Specifically, Benson has been eager to learn and never afraid to ask questions in the meeting room.
“Kahlil is a hell of a football player, tons of talent,” Moore said Thursday. “It obviously put him in the position he is now to be able to go out and start his first NFL game. I mean, it’s awesome to see.”
So how did Benson slip through the cracks to go undrafted after starting at right tackle for last year’s national champion in Indiana? The answer is complex, considering Benson has good size at 6 feet 6, 319 pounds and tested well athletically.
The simplest explanation: Benson’s tape was inconsistent. That included the national championship game against Miami, when Benson posted a 34.6 Pro Football Focus offensive grade — the lowest mark on the team.
Scouting reports also had concerns about his production. The Athletic ’s Dane Brugler, who listed Benson as the 29th-best offensive tackle in his class, noted he had “sloppy tendencies that he must continue to address” while correctly predicting his size and length would “give him a chance in a pro camp.”
Benson also had some previous knee concerns. His indirect college path could’ve hurt him, too, as he transferred from Indiana to Colorado, then back to Indiana before finally solidifying himself at right tackle in his final season.
Something that can’t be questioned now? How quickly Benson stood out once he got to Kansas City.
The team strategically holds its camp the week after the draft for this reason. It’s a rush to get guys in, but it also gives the Chiefs a first glance at prospects they might end up signing.
If Kansas City had waited an extra week for rookie minicamp, and Benson had impressed elsewhere? There’s a good chance he’d be wearing a different uniform.
“Each day, he got better and better. And by the end of the day, you’ve seen a big, strong kid (who’s) got some ability,” Bradway said. “So let’s just sign him to the 90-man.”
Benson continued to take off after that point. He started with the third-team offensive line in organized team activities before separating himself. Soon, he was with the second string, then briefly at mandatory minicamp, he got looks with the first-team offense while being inserted into the competition for the right-tackle job.
“I didn’t let the naysayers really say too much,” Benson told reporters Aug. 12. “I kept my head down and kept driving forward.”
That’s led to a potential opportunity under the brightest of lights.
Benson is set to start his pro career on “Monday Night Football” against the Denver Broncos, who have one of the NFL’s top defensive lines. He’ll also be tasked with protecting quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ blind side in his first game back after December knee surgery.
When talking about Benson on Thursday, Reid said he hoped he’d play with the idealistic swagger many young employees have when they first get hired.
“I want his confidence to be that and go out and play and just use his abilities,” Reid said, “and write a good story.”
Bradway acknowledges that Benson’s path was rare as he established himself with the Chiefs.
Sometimes a scouting department deserves praise for unearthing a hidden talent. Or seeing potential in someone the rest of the NFL missed.
With Benson specifically, though? The Chiefs get credit for making a call and bringing him to Kansas City.
From there, though, he’s done the rest.
“He doesn’t carry himself like a tryout guy,” Bradway said. “He knew he belonged.”

full_text:
Sean McVay called the season-opening loss to the 49ers 'a humbling day.' Robert Cianflone / Getty Images
MELBOURNE, Australia — For 15 months, the Los Angeles Rams devised a plan to dominate an Australia game in just 30 hours between flights.
It took two plays for that plan to fall apart.
The Rams were halfway across the world and 17 hours from the SoFi Stadium backdrop they gave up to make this trip for the NFL’s first regular-season game in Australia. What they needed was to hit a slant pass to Puka Nacua to pull within a field goal of the San Francisco 49ers in the third quarter, so Matthew Stafford fired the ball into his go-to receiver’s gut, only for Nacua to fall short of the end zone.
On fourth down, coach Sean McVay called for Stafford to run a quarterback sneak. And then he hit a brick wall for a turnover on downs.
Then the 49ers drove 99 yards on the Rams’ retooled and star-studded defense to add yet another touchdown.
A hallmark moment became an international embarrassment on Friday morning at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, where the Rams suffered a 27-7 loss to the rival 49ers.
It was their first defeat by more than one score since the 2024 season, when Saquon Barkley and the Philadelphia Eagles ran all over them. It was also the fewest points they’d ever scored in a game with Stafford at quarterback.
“This is a humbling day for us,” McVay said. “… I make no excuses. Whether you want to say it’s about travel or whatever, we just weren’t good enough in that window.”
The Rams placed a bet that flying in the day before an Australian game in order to not change body clocks could have them at their best. After all, that’s what worked so brilliantly for them last October in London, when they flew in the day before from Baltimore, kept their Eastern Time-adjusted body clocks and rolled in a 9:30 a.m. ET start to win 35-7 over the Jacksonville Jaguars in a game that gave birth to their identity of three-tight end sets.
But this moment was inherently different: The body clock shift was 17 hours rather than five. The flight was 16 hours rather than seven. The setting would come in Week 1, after no preseason for their starters, rather than packed in the middle of the schedule and right before a bye week as the London game was.
Rather than see themselves at their best, the Rams found themselves at their worst in Australia. They ended up flying 32 hours in three days just to take their worst loss in a year and a half.
It was the opposite approach of the 49ers, who turned the week into an experience for the players and a chance to reset body clocks to Australian time. San Francisco must now fight the effects of trying to reset those body clocks back to Pacific Time ahead of the final 16 games, and perhaps that’s Los Angeles’ edge in never changing at all. It’s possible that’s the trade-off in these two disparate approaches.
“I know everyone’s going to make a huge deal about that and be asking about the travel s—,” wide receiver Davante Adams said. “That had nothing to do with it. We just have to play better.”
Even if the Rams don’t want to admit that their travel plan played a role in this outcome, they need that to be true. They need a Week 1 game in Australia to be an anomaly of circumstance and planning errors, at a time when costs were higher given that their starters skipped the entire preseason.
Because the alternative is what they can’t have become true. The 2026 Rams can’t resemble anything as they did here.
That cannot be the connection they’ll see from Stafford and Adams. Last year, it wasn’t smooth out of the gate, but they found a way to become a red zone cheat code as Adams led the league with 14 receiving touchdowns and Stafford won his first MVP. In Melbourne, the two connected just three times on six tries for 26 yards. Stafford managed 155 yards on 25 attempts and did not throw a touchdown pass, one year after he piled up an NFL-best 46.
“It’s just Week 1 stuff that you deal with sometimes,” Adams added. “It’s not an excuse, but there’s certain times you have to feel them out and get a good feel for what the defense and what they’re doing based on what we were running.”
That cannot be the tight end room they see this season, either. After all, that was the group that revolutionized last year’s offense from strong but static to unpredictable, setting a league-wide trend with 13 personnel and dominating on play action and in the run game with defenses consistently compromised.
This offseason, that group added a second-round pick to the group in Max Klare and got excited about a Year 2 breakout for Terrance Ferguson. In Melbourne, Klare was inactive, Ferguson didn’t catch a pass and no tight end finished with more than 13 yards.
That can’t be the secondary approach they’ll take this season, either. The Rams made that group a focus to overhaul after last season and targeted physical, man-coverage cornerbacks in Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson, who won two Super Bowls together as outside cornerbacks on the Kansas City Chiefs.
But against the 49ers, the Rams ran man coverage on just 13.9 percent of plays as opposed to 77 percent in zone coverage, according to Summer Sport research. As a result, Brock Purdy finished with a 73.5 percent completion rate, three touchdown passes and a 105.6 quarterback rating, and Watson was too often on the receiving end.
The Rams did secure one interception of Purdy, when Quentin Lake drifted back into zone and Purdy tried to force a ball to Mike Evans. The Rams defense celebrated by pretending to take a nap, a shot the 49ers would throw back at them in a postgame victory tweet with the caption, “Sleep tight.”
That can’t be the version of pass-rush support they’ll put around Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald. Garrett was neutralized, and Donald was back at home after opting to wait another week to make his return from a two-year retirement. Without that superstar impact, the Rams managed no sacks and just two quarterback hits on 39 dropbacks.
They had moments like the one in the second quarter, where they rushed four players, with Braden Fiske and Desjuan Johnson rotating in. The 49ers didn’t even run play action, and Purdy didn’t see a body around him as he completed a seven-step drop and found Demarcus Robinson on a deep post for a 39-yard touchdown.
“From start to finish, I just don’t feel like we were locked in and focused,” outside linebacker Byron Young said.
That can’t be the version of Garrett the Rams get, either. He was the one most noticeably not himself, consistently checking in and out of the game and lacking his normal burst after missing weeks of training camp with a swollen knee. He finished outside of the box score, too, with zero tackles, sacks, quarterback hits or tackles for loss.
“This was the worst version of myself that I’ve put out there,” Garrett said. “I’ve got to be better. I’ve got to find a way to recover and get back to the player I know that I can be and that I’ve shown I’ve been before. … When I was out there, I was a little bit more focused on myself and trying to stay healthy than what they were doing, and it showed. I wasn’t where I needed to be for my team.”
The list of Rams players who looked themselves in Melbourne was rather light. McDuffie flew around to make plays in the run and pass games, including the rep in the red zone where he blanketed a much larger George Kittle and nearly reeled in an interception. Blake Corum showed strong vision and improving speed, finishing with 54 yards on 10 carries.
The good news is that so many parts can go so much better. And they’ll have to.
Nacua can get back to taking over games. The tight ends can get back to blurring the run and the pass, with Stafford at the controls and Kyren Williams and Corum wearing defenses down between the tackles. Adams will score touchdowns, allowing the Rams to build leads their opponents have to answer by dropping back against Garrett, Young, Kobie Turner and Donald, and throwing at McDuffie, Lake,…

title: Kirk Cousins is the starter for now — what can he do for a new-look Raiders offense? The 38-year-old can't match Fernando Mendoza's physical traits, but he knows how to survive. Sam Warren 2

full_text:
Kirk Cousins will be behind center when the Raiders open the season against the Dolphins. Kenneth Richmond / Getty Images
HENDERSON, Nev. — Kirk Cousins wants to stay present. When asked about what a successful 2026 season looks like for him, he said it starts with focusing “on the here and now.”
Last week, Klint Kubiak named Cousins his starter for Sunday’s opener against the Miami Dolphins, the veteran winning the competition over No. 1 draft pick Fernando Mendoza. It’s a significant accomplishment for Cousins considering he lost his starting job with the Atlanta Falcons less than two seasons ago. It wasn’t clear he’d get another opportunity to start in the NFL, and the 38-year-old didn’t relish having to earn another shot with a different team, saying that winning the job was never an end goal.
“It’s less important to me than what you do after that first snap,” Cousins said. “I think it’s all about this entire season and winning the long game, and not just about the start of the season.”
Much has been made of the Raiders’ quarterback succession plan. The veteran will eventually cede to the rookie, and a new era for the franchise will begin. In the meantime, the Raiders believe Cousins will create a path for Mendoza to follow.
“When (quarterbacks) have a guy in front of them that they can look up to and they can see how something’s done, that’s going to accelerate their growth,” Kubiak said.
Kubiak said Cousins is “starting for a reason.” Given Cousins’ age and struggles in Atlanta, there are justifiable questions about how long he’ll be able to hold off Mendoza — and exactly what he’ll provide the Raiders while he is QB1.
Kubiak said leadership and command of the offense were the biggest areas of improvement for Cousins during his first few months with the Raiders..
Cousins has expertise that can be learned only from playing 15 years in the NFL. Those seasons were spent in offshoots of the Shanahan-style offense the Raiders are running, including three with the Minnesota Vikings when Kubiak was his position coach and, eventually, his play caller. Cousins said there was “plenty I needed to learn” when he reunited with the coach, but his foundational knowledge has allowed him to take “total ownership” of the offense. Such is what this Raiders staff is looking for.
“Complete the football, get us into the right plays, get us out of bad plays, don’t make bad plays worse,” offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko said of Cousins’ tasks. “I don’t think the blueprint has ever changed with the way we ask our quarterbacks to play.”
The Raiders didn’t lose yardage on any of Cousins’ 30 snaps in the preseason, and they seldom did during training-camp practices. Much of that was thanks to Cousins’ ability to get the ball out quickly.
Cousins averaged a 2.32-second time to throw during the preseason, third fastest among quarterbacks with 10 or more attempts and nearly a half-second faster than the league average from last season (2.76 seconds), according to TruMedia. He was decisive, stayed in rhythm and navigated his reads smoothly; all vital for a quarterback in Kubiak’s timing-based offense. Conversely, Mendoza averaged 2.95 seconds to throw on his preseason attempts, 12th slowest among quarterbacks with 10 or more attempts.
Cousins’ quick release allows him to avoid sacks — particularly notable considering the Raiders allowed a league-high 64 last year. The additions of center Tyler Linderbaum and offensive line coach Rick Dennison mean the Raiders should have better pass protection, but getting the ball out quickly will lighten the offensive line’s burden.
Cousins also displayed his mastery at the line of scrimmage. He regularly checked play calls after surveying the defense. The Raiders have been pleased with Mendoza’s growth in that area, but it will be a while before he can match the veteran’s pre-snap acumen.
On Cousins’ first preseason drive, he found himself in a third-and-long situation against the Arizona Cardinals, who were signaling a heavy blitz with seven defenders showing a pass rush. He checked the play to keep tight end Michael Mayer and running back Ashton Jeanty in on protection to match the pressure. The switch gave Cousins adequate protection, and he hit receiver Jack Bech on an out route for a first down.
Kirk Cousins and Jack Bech fine-tuning their connection ‼️
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/7HmrW03EZO
— NFL (@NFL) August 14, 2026
“He’s going to get us in the right checks,” Mayer said. “He’s going to get us in the right formations. That’s what I expect out of him. I think that’s what everybody expects out of him in this locker room.”
With Cousins under center, expect a quick, clinical operation. Cousins’ decisiveness and awareness are key traits Las Vegas wants Mendoza to observe and learn to emulate.
While Cousins has displayed the skills that make Kubiak’s offense thrive, his lack of elite physical traits also limits it.
Cousins was never known for his arm strength or athleticism, and now he’s 38 and a few years removed from a torn Achilles tendon. The football has less zip coming from his hand than Mendoza’s.
Cousins was intercepted multiple times in training camp by defenders undercutting targeted routes. Then in the preseason finale, he was nearly picked off by San Francisco 49ers cornerback Jack Jones breaking on a slant to tight end Brock Bowers — normally a sure completion given the matchup. Cousins was in rhythm but, throwing off his back foot, didn’t give the throw nearly enough juice.
Cousins has had similar issues since the Achilles tear. His 16 interceptions with the Falcons in 2024 were tied for most in the NFL and set a career high. He threw five last season in eight starts.
The Raiders have consequently kept things close to the line of scrimmage with Cousins on the field. He averaged 2.9 air yards per attempt during the preseason. Only Atlanta’s Tua Tagovailoa had a shorter average depth of target among quarterbacks with 10 or more attempts, according to TruMedia. Just one of Cousins’ 17 preseason pass attempts traveled 10 or more yards downfield (the completion to Bech).
Preseason is not an accurate representation of a team’s regular-season game plan, and the small sample size isn’t enough to sound alarms. But the lack of deep throws takes away a key component of Kubiak’s success.
Under Kubiak’s control in 2025, the Seattle Seahawks thrived on explosive passing plays. Their 57 completions for 20-plus yards were eighth most in the league, and they were tied for the most 40-plus yard receptions (12). Last year, Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold averaged 7.8 air yards per attempt. Given Kubiak’s commitment to the run game, play action sets up deep shots. And the threat of a downfield passing game also aids the ground game.
That approach is much more similar to the one Kubiak and Cousins used when they were in Minnesota. The Vikings’ 63 pass plays of 20-plus yards were fifth most in the NFL in 2021, Kubiak’s lone year as offensive coordinator. Cousins averaged 7.7 air yards per attempt that season. As far as this preseason goes, Mendoza was more in line with previous Kubiak quarterbacks, averaging 6.6 air yards per attempt and showing off his arm strength with big plays to receivers Malik Benson and Jalen Nailor.
If Cousins can’t present the threat of the deep ball, opposing defenses can consistently play man coverage, hindering the success of the offense no matter how well he operates it. Teams can focus on stopping the run, putting pressure on Cousins to drive passes downfield to keep the Raiders moving. Las Vegas can call on the veteran to do so, but they risk putting the ball in harm’s way, especially with a lack of separators at receiver.
Cousins still has the mental intangibles that the Raiders are looking for in their signal caller. Yet physically, he might not provide what’s needed to unleash Kubiak’s scheme. The Raiders have made clear that they won’t rush Mendoza, but it might not take long before it’s clear…

Anticipation crescendos ahead of every season for the Minnesota Vikings, but this year’s opener offers extra suspense.

full_text:
Kyler Murray is set to make his regular-season debut for the Vikings on Sunday against the Packers. John Jones / Imagn Images
Anticipation crescendos ahead of every season for the Minnesota Vikings, but this year’s opener offers extra suspense.
First and foremost, the Vikings will unveil a new quarterback in Kyler Murray. Throw in the opponent being the rival Green Bay Packers, and it becomes easy to understand the buzz.
What will happen Sunday afternoon inside U.S. Bank Stadium? For the fifth straight season, The Athletic ’s Alec Lewis and Jon Krawczynski are here for an all-encompassing preview.
Lewis: The trenches. I’ll leave the low-hanging (but incredibly relevant) quarterback fruit for Jon. For me, the most important aspects of this game for the Vikings are the performances of the offensive and defensive lines. Minnesota revamped its rushing attack this offseason. Coach Kevin O’Connell continuously discussed the Vikings’ changes, and Sunday presents the first real opportunity to show their impact. Without Micah Parsons, the Packers’ defensive front looks susceptible. The same goes for the other side of the football. The Vikings loved the progression of Dallas Turner in training camp. Green Bay’s sketchy offensive-line availability and talent could open the door for Turner and the rest of the defensive line to make an introductory statement.
Krawczynski: Was that a short joke? I can’t reach the high-hanging fruit is what you’re saying? SMH. It be your own people sometimes.
Of course I’ll be watching Kyler Murray. The Vikings went 9-8 last season while enduring a QB carousel that was among the worst in the league. Murray does not need to be 2009 Brett Favre or even 2024 Sam Darnold, though it would be nice if that happened. If he is simply a really good quarterback, that would go such a long way toward helping this team make a playoff run. I’ll be watching to see how he handles the emotions of a Packers game in the season opener. This is, literally, a golden opportunity for him. Put together a strong season, and he’ll cement himself as a longtime starter making big money. If he struggles, life as a backup could be here sooner than later. How will he handle the magnitude of the moment?
Lewis: Turnovers. O’Connell took over in 2022, and since then, the Vikings have turned the ball over 108 times. That is tied for second-most in the NFL behind the Cleveland Browns. The Vikings are 35-4 under O’Connell when they break even or win the turnover margin — the highest winning percentage of any team in the NFL over those four years. Conversely, the Packers are at the opposite end of the spectrum. They have turned the ball over only 72 times since 2022. This continues to be the most predictive statistic of wins and losses, and it ties to the first note about the trenches. Remain efficient at running the football, and the Vikings can mitigate risk.
Krawczynski: Jordan Love. I’ll admit that I have gone hot and cold on Love over the last couple of years. There are moments when he looks terrific, the NFL’s next great gunslinger. Then there are moments he is really underwhelming. I’m not super high on his receivers, but, man, he throws a beautiful ball. He has had months to prepare for this game and has experience going against Brian Flores. If Love is on his game, it also puts much more pressure on Murray to be great. A double-edged sword.
Lewis: Kyler Murray versus Jonathan Gannon’s defense. Not only did the Vikings draw a Packers team with a new defensive coordinator in Gannon, but Gannon’s history with Murray also adds a dimension to the matchup. On Thursday, Vikings offensive coordinator Wes Phillips talked about preparing for Sunday by watching tape from Gannon’s time in Philadelphia and Arizona. Gannon’s strategy will likely revolve around his strong personnel at safety with Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams. But how he thinks he can attack his former quarterback, a player he said he respects, will be interesting to see.
Krawczynski: Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason versus Green Bay’s front seven. I’m gonna zag a little on Alec here because I’ve found it interesting just how intentional O’Connell has been all offseason when discussing the importance of the running game. J.J. McCarthy could have used a similar commitment last season. I don’t know if it would have changed his story, but it was clear he needed a strong ground game to support him, and the Vikings were 23rd in rushing offense. Some of that was due to the injuries on the offensive line, but some of it could be attributable to O’Connell’s approach as a play caller as well. At any rate, the changes he made on the coaching staff and the extra emphasis he has put on the running game this preseason are encouraging. Staying committed to that against a Parsons-less Packers front will be key to keeping Love off the field and helping Murray settle in at quarterback.
Lewis: What is the Vikings’ ceiling in 2026? With improved quarterback play and a healthy offensive line, the offense should dramatically improve. There are still defensive questions, especially from a durability standpoint. But Flores has proved he will maximize his personnel. This leaves the team’s potential in a bit of a gray area. The organization has not won a playoff game since 2019. O’Connell is entering his fifth season at the helm. Superstar receiver Justin Jefferson is 27 and in the middle of his prime. Reaching the playoffs seems realistic, but can they go even further?
Here is where each team ranked in 2025 in the following categories, using explosive play rate for explosiveness, success rate for efficiency and DVOA’s strength of schedule:
Lewis: 24-20 Vikings. Cornerback tackling might be the most underrated aspect of the game for Minnesota. Find a way to limit run-after-catch opportunities for Green Bay’s wideouts, avoid turnovers offensively and Minnesota should be able to ride a raucous crowd to a Week 1 victory.
Krawczynski: 23-21 Packers. Here is the good news, Vikings fans: I don’t have a great feeling about this season. I’m concerned about the quarterback, the secondary and their lack of depth across the board should injuries pile up. Why is that good news? Because every time I seem to be pessimistic about their chances, they put together a really good season. This is one of the most well-coached teams in the league. They need the talent to match their brainpower. Really looking forward to this one. Let’s never start the season this late again.

full_text:
On 25 designed rushing plays against the Seahawks on Wednesday night, the Patriots gained just 65 yards, an average of 2.6 yards per carry. Jane Gershovich / Getty Images
New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel didn’t hide from quarterback Drake Maye’s struggles on Thursday afternoon after a red-eye, cross-country flight back from Seattle following his team’s season-opening loss to the Seahawks.
“Drake will learn from it, and hopefully we’ll be better for it in the end,” Vrabel said.
The head coach lauded improvements from the offensive line, said the running game got better in the second half and refused to throw receiver Romeo Doubs under the bus, noting that drops sometimes happen.
But there was plenty more to glean from the Patriots’ first game. Here are 10 thoughts on where the team stands and what’s to come.
1. There were plenty of concerning takeaways from the Patriots’ season-opening dud, but none have the long-term ramifications of A.J. Brown’s reported high-ankle sprain that could keep him out of several games.
The Patriots felt all offseason that wide receiver was one position where they had plenty of depth. But that feels very different after Brown’s injury and Doubs’ struggles in his debut.
Kayshon Boutte was obviously frustrated by his situation, and it was understandable that the Patriots traded him. But we’re one game into the season, and the offense could already use someone like Boutte.
This is going to put a lot on the plate of Kyle Williams. Even though his only preseason success came on straight go balls that didn’t test his route running, coaches have professed faith in the 2025 third-round pick. Well, now we’re going to see how ready Williams is for a bigger role.
2. In the Super Bowl, it felt like the Patriots lost for a ton of reasons — but not because of Drake Maye. What could he have possibly done in that game as the Pats were outmanned in every area?
But after this opener, it feels like they lost because of Maye.
The first two interceptions weren’t great, but the third one was truly incomprehensible.
As a 22-year-old rookie, Maye showed great maturity in handling a brutal situation. Last season, Maye showed great poise in making spectacular plays behind a struggling O-line. The Pats felt he’d keep growing this season and become a master of game situations.
And then on Wednesday night, he made perhaps the worst play of his young career in the biggest moment.
The play design was supposed to lead to a quick throw to Hunter Henry. If it wasn’t there, he should have thrown the ball away and moved on. At the very least, overtime seemed secured with a very makeable field goal. Instead, he threw a horrible pass off his back foot that was intercepted in the end zone.
It was a shocking way for Maye to start a season with MVP hopes.
3. It was a brutal way for the Patriots to start the season, despite being underdogs. That’s because they failed to do the one thing Vrabel harped on during his first year with the franchise. They didn’t take advantage of bad football.
Between the injury to Sam Darnold and a myriad of bad penalties, it was like the Seahawks were trying to give that game away. An illegal shift wiped off a go-ahead touchdown for them late in the third quarter. An offside penalty wiped away a drive-extending tush push. The Seahawks had 10 total penalties.
The Patriots have to win games like that.
4. What did we learn about the Patriots defense? It looks like it’s going to lean on the blitz again.
Last season, Zak Kuhr turned to the blitz to try to make up for a struggling pass rush. The hope this season was that he wouldn’t have to lean on it as much.
But that wasn’t the case against the Seahawks. The Patriots blitzed on a third of their snaps, a figure that would’ve been the second-highest blitz rate in the NFL last season (behind only Brian Flores’ unit in Minnesota).
5. It’s hard to know how much stock to put into that defensive performance considering it was mostly against backup quarterback Drew Lock.
The good: Christian Gonzalez is still a stud, the secondary was good with the exception of a Craig Woodson missed tackle on Jaxon Smith-Njigba’s 44-yard touchdown and rookie Gabe Jacas notched a sack and looked the part.
The bad: The pass rush didn’t get home without blitzing, the run defense struggled and the linebackers didn’t have a great night.
6. One positive from the defense was the play of Dre’Mont Jones, who recorded a team-high six pressures. He’ll have to play well while Jacas develops and with Harold Landry out, and he did his part Wednesday.
On the flip side, the Patriots are going to need more from Elijah Ponder opposite Jones.
7. One positive from the offense was the play of Will Campbell. All offseason, he heard about his playoff struggles after his knee injuries. But coaches expressed confidence in him and he backed it up against a talented Seahawks D-line. He allowed only two pressures and looked ready to take a step forward in Year 2.
8. The New England running game has to be better. On 25 designed rushing plays against the Seahawks, the Pats gained just 65 yards, an average of 2.6 yards per carry.
Maybe it’s fair to give them a slight pass against a Seattle defense that stopped the run better than anyone last season. But it has to get better next week against the Pittsburgh Steelers, who ranked 24th in rushing EPA per play allowed last season.
The Patriots averaged 0.07 rushing yards before contact, which would’ve been easily the worst mark in the league last season. So it was more of a run-blocking thing against the Seahawks than a case of backs missing open lanes.
9. The other frustrating part about the New England run game was the way it was called so conservatively by offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels.
Even against an elite run defense, McDaniels called 17 percent more running plays on first down than league average. Predictably, those rushes rarely gained meaningful yards.
The Patriots had an early-down success rate of just 24 percent (again, a figure that would’ve been the lowest in the league last season), often putting them in second-and-long and third-and-long situations.
And yet, they kept going back to first-down runs that didn’t work.
10. Jacas showed strides as he tried to make up for lost time, having missed all of spring practices plus the start of training camp. He notched a sack Wednesday night and drew a compliment from his head coach.
“Continues to improve,” Vrabel said Thursday. “He was active, set some good edges in the run game. … I thought it was an improvement.”

full_text:
New York Giants coach John Harbaugh vowed to build a team good enough “to kick the Cowboys’ ass." Yannick Peterhans / Imagn Images
John Harbaugh led the Baltimore Ravens for 18 years in one of the NFL’s fiercest rivalries with the Pittsburgh Steelers. Now, in his first year as New York Giants coach, Harbaugh is jumping into another storied rivalry with his first game against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football.
Harbaugh added some spice to the rivalry when he vowed to build a team good enough “to kick the Cowboys’ ass” at the Giants’ Town Hall event in May. Harbaugh’s words were delivered to a fan base desperate for a reversal of the one-sided rivalry. The Cowboys are 16-2 in the series since the start of 2017 season.
Naturally, the Cowboys caught wind of Harbaugh’s comment, prompting wide receiver CeeDee Lamb to respond, “lol that’s cute,” on Instagram. Harbaugh said he loved Lamb’s comeback.
“It was cute,” Harbaugh said. “Comeback was cute, too. So it was good.”
Harbaugh’s arrival has ushered in a more confident vibe. Team co-owner Chris Mara voiced the change in tone in a recent interview with ESPN New York .
“The way I look at it is we’ve used the word ‘hope’ in the last 10 or 12 years or whatever it might be,” Mara said. “The hope now has turned into expectations. At least for me it has. I don’t hope we win this year. I expect it. And I think everybody else does, too.”
This is all a breath of fresh air after the previous regime of coach Brian Daboll and general manager Joe Schoen ran from expectations heading into every season. Schoen remains, and he said last week he expects “to be competitive week in and week out.”
The Giants were competitive last season. That wasn’t good enough. Their failure to finish games led to a 4-13 record and a coaching change.
The expectation should be for the Giants to win immediately under Harbaugh. Schoen has had four years to build the roster, and the “young nucleus of talent” he assembled was both the reason he was retained and why this job appealed to Harbaugh.
For as poor as Dave Gettleman’s four-year tenure was as GM, the roster he left was led to the playoffs by Daboll in 2022. This is now the fifth year of Schoen’s roster build, so similar results should be expected, especially with an upgrade at coach.
“Meritocracy” was a buzzword during training camp that Harbaugh has backed up. The Giants cut wide receiver Darius Slayton , whose $16 million cap hit was the fourth highest on the team, on Monday. Cornerback Paulson Adebo, who has a team-high $24.2 million cap hit, will likely open the season as a backup behind Greg Newsome II and Deonte Banks.
The longest-tenured Giant, Slayton had $9.75 million of his $12.25 million salary fully guaranteed, so the financial benefits of dumping him were minimal. The Giants clearly were hoping to trade Slayton, but they couldn’t find any takers for his hefty salary. Harbaugh declined to answer when asked whether the Giants tried to get Slayton to take a pay cut, but that would have been a non-starter based on his guarantees.
So, the Giants held onto Slayton until cutting ties six days before the season opener. The final $2.5 million of Slayton’s salary would have become guaranteed if he was on the roster for the opener. The Giants gained $3 million in cap space this year by cutting Slayton, but that will count as $3 million in dead money on next year’s cap.
Harbaugh explained the decision by stating that he watches practice every day and noted that Slayton may still not be 100 percent healthy from the sports hernia surgery he underwent in the spring. Slayton was trending toward being a healthy scratch for the opener, and Harbaugh clearly didn’t believe the veteran could help the team.
Even if that’s the case now, Harbaugh may regret discarding a player who has averaged 633.6 yards per season if injuries strike at receiver. But Slayton’s release drives home the message that every player needs to earn his spot.
There would be no financial benefit from cutting Adebo, whose $17.25 million base salary this season is fully guaranteed. And even though he had a disappointing offseason, the Giants’ cornerback situation eliminated that from being a consideration. Banks has performed well to earn a starting spot opposite Newsome. But Banks’ track record makes it impossible to count on him to consistently perform at a high level. So Adebo, who raised his play as training camp progressed, will likely open the season as an expensive backup.
The Giants extended two veterans on Sunday: backup quarterback Jameis Winston and left guard Jon Runyan. The two-year, $12 million extension for Winston was a no-brainer. His $6.5 million average salary slots him between Washington’s Marcus Mariota ($7 million) and Cincinnati’s Joe Flacco ($6 million). Winston’s arm talent makes him a viable backup, and he’s proven to be a respected leader.
Runyan’s two-year, $22 million extension was more surprising. Runyan had a $9 million base salary with no guarantees in the final year of the three-year, $30 million contract he signed in 2024. That made him a potential salary cap casualty this offseason, but the seventh-year veteran clearly won over the coaching staff.
Runyan has been an average guard, and his pay reflects that. It would be understandable to desire an upgrade, but the early extension has removed a potential need in free agency. The best impending free agents, like Indianapolis’ Quenton Nelson, often get re-signed before reaching the market, which drives up the price on the next tier.
By locking in Runyan at $11 million per year, the Giants likely won’t dip into the guard market next offseason. But there’s nothing stopping them from drafting a long-term upgrade. In fact, that might be the ideal route if that’s how their draft board plays out. They can roll with Runyan for next season while the young guard develops. They could then reassess after next season, continuing with Runyan for the final year of his extension or cutting ties with only $3 million in dead money on the 2028 salary cap.
The Giants now have Runyan and right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor, who signed a three-year, $39 million extension in March, under contract through 2028. Left tackle Andrew Thomas and rookie right guard Francis Mauigoa are signed through 2029. Only center is unsettled, with John Michael Schmitz playing n the final year of his contract.
There finally seems to be a plan to the offensive line build, with the Giants investing Day 3 picks in players who aren’t rushed into the lineup. The Giants have 2025 fifth-round pick Marcus Mbow and 2026 sixth-round pick JC Davis developing as potential successors to Eluemunor. The Giants also could shift Mbow and/or Davis inside. Extending Runyan allows the Giants to build a similar pipeline at guard.
The biggest question heading into Sunday’s season opener is the status of wide receiver Malik Nabers . It has been a long road for Nabers, who tore his ACL and meniscus on Sept. 28 last year. He underwent a second surgery in the spring to remove scar tissue that was causing stiffness in his knee.
The team remained hopeful throughout the lengthy rehab process that Nabers would be ready for the opener, and his workload during the preseason was structured to keep him on that timeline. Nabers has passed every checkpoint along the way, fully participating in practice Wednesday and Thursday.
Still, there have been no assurances Nabers will play on Sunday night. Part of that is gamesmanship. Harbaugh pointedly declared that he’s not sharing who will play in the game for competitive reasons.
But Harbaugh did say, “I think he’s ready to go.” The question comes down to how ready Nabers feels.
“If he’s ready to go and he feels like he’s ready to go, then he’ll play,” Harbaugh said. “If he’s not and he’s not ready, then he won’t play. That’s how it works.”
Nabers emphasized Thursday that the decision is in his hands. He said he needs 100 percent confidence that he can perform at his…

full_text:
Robert Saleh makes his Titans regular-season debut Sunday against his former team. Kyle Terada / Imagn Images
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — Robert Saleh used to explain the dichotomy of week-to-week reactions in the NFL this way:
If you lose, it’s the apocalypse.
If you win, you’re going to the Super Bowl.
Of course, he didn’t really mean the NFL. He meant coaching in this market, for this team, the New York Jets.
With that mindset, the end of the world has been a near-weekly occurrence in Florham Park every fall. But Sunday’s season opener, going up against a Tennessee Titans team now led by Saleh, has a more doomsday feel than usual for the Jets.
The reasons aren’t difficult to figure out. On one hand, you have Aaron Glenn, coming off a brutal debut season. After a 3-14 year that ended in five straight losses by a historic margin, Glenn fired half his coaching staff and took over defensive play-calling himself. Ask anyone outside the Jets building which NFL head coach is on the hottest seat, and Glenn might be their answer.
On the other hand, Glenn is going against Saleh, a ghost of the Jets’ past, the one that owner Woody Johnson fired unceremoniously less than two years ago. Johnson picked Glenn to replace him and to fix the problems of the previous regime. The Jets have a multi-year plan to get back on track, but the first year was undoubtedly a failure.
Glenn losing to the man he replaced, and the Jets losing to a Titans team few expect to be competitive this season, would be hard to process for a fan base already overwhelmed by reminders that their team hasn’t made the playoffs since 2010.
It does feel fitting that the Jets will have to defeat Saleh to avoid the so-called apocalypse. Though Glenn doesn’t care much about who is on the other sideline.
“I get it, it goes with … the territory of Saleh once being here and then I step in as the head coach,” Glenn said. “But to me, I look at it as if it’s a game that we’re going out there to win and it doesn’t matter who it is. That’s the mindset of these players, that’s the mindset of this coaching staff, that’s the mindset of this organization. Our job is to go out there and play this game and be the best that we can be on every play and to go out there and win a game. Nothing else is to be thought of.”
Saleh has struck a similar tone.
“New York is still a special place, gave me my first opportunity as a head coach,” Saleh told reporters last week. “(But) our desire to beat the Jets is because it’s Week 1 and nothing more. I’m forever grateful for all the opportunity they gave me. I don’t hold grudges.”
Even if Saleh won’t say it publicly, it would be fair to assume he’s carrying a little something extra this week — for Glenn and, especially, for Johnson. Saleh went 20-36 as Jets coach and has often viewed Johnson as the biggest reason for the issues of his tenure. Ultimately, he and Johnson never saw eye to eye.
As for Glenn: Even if he hasn’t talked much about Saleh directly, he did take some not-so-subtle shots at him during training camp last summer, including moments where he pointed out how often the Jets were penalized previously and how the biggest reason Will McDonald hadn’t taken a leap forward yet was “coaching.” Some carryover Jets players from Saleh’s roster, like Breece Hall and Garrett Wilson, alluded to “instability” and a lack of accountability from the previous staff too.
Clearly, that’s not the view of everyone who played for Saleh in New York — otherwise so many of them wouldn’t have joined him in Nashville. Since he was hired last year, Saleh’s Titans have added eight former Jets to the active roster or practice squad, including John Franklin-Myers, Jermaine Johnson, Solomon Thomas, Jacob Martin, Tony Adams, Isaiah Oliver, Jalyn Holmes and Michael Carter IV — and they worked out two more (Xavier Gipson and Jason Brownlee) this week. Saleh also has three assistants from his Jets staff (Tony Oden, Marquand Manuel and Aaron Whitecotton) and another (Tanzel Smart) who played for the Jets when Saleh was there.
Thomas recently told reporters in Tennessee that he didn’t feel like the problems in New York were Saleh’s fault — though it should be noted that Thomas played for Saleh in San Francisco and the two are close.
“Just the fact that he has so many former Jets here just shows that guys love playing for him. They know what he’s about to do here and they want to be a part of it,” Thomas said. “I think there was such a disconnect based on what was portrayed from the front office to the locker room. I don’t really like talking about anything other than football. But I’ve never really been in a place where more was said out of the front office than out of the locker room. And said as a distraction. And it was really unfortunate because our locker room was really the opposite of what was going on in the front office.”
The Titans, clearly, are using Saleh’s past as motivation for Sunday.
“It means everything to us,” quarterback Cam Ward told reporters. “We want to win not only for ourselves and the culture we’re setting but we want to win for him too.”
The few Jets remaining from the Saleh era have mostly downplayed the significance of going against their old coach. There are only five men left on defense, and only one of them is a projected Week 1 starter: linebacker Jamien Sherwood. (The others: edge rusher Will McDonald, cornerback Qwan’tez Stiggers, edge rusher Braiden McGregor and linebacker Marcelino McCrary-Ball.) On offense, Wilson, Hall, left tackle Olu Fashanu, guard Joe Tippmann and running backs Braelon Allen and Isaiah Davis all played under Saleh.
“It doesn’t matter who the competition is or who is on the other side of the ball,” Sherwood said. “Football is football. I’m gonna be playing against some of the people I started with but they’re not here anymore.”
Most of the conversation about Saleh has centered more on the kind of defense he’ll be running than any sort of emotional energy they’re carrying about going against him almost two years after he was fired in-season.
“I’m sure he’s got some wrinkles in there since he’s been here,” Wilson said. “It’s (a defense) that I’ve seen. They’re always sound in what they do. I know the way he teaches it. He’s a thorough man — I’m excited for the challenge.”
Offensive coordinator Frank Reich called it an “aggressive” defense. “Traditionally, he has been on-point and has earned the reputation for being one of the better defensive minds,” Reich said. “They have a unique style and brand of play. It’ll be a good challenge for us.”
The Jets haven’t fared particularly well when facing a previous head coach for the first time. In 2019, the Jets lost to the Buccaneers, led by Todd Bowles. They lost to the Rex Ryan Bills twice in 2015. They beat the Eric Mangini-led Browns in 2010 and the Herm Edwards-led Chiefs in overtime in 2007. They lost by 11 to the Bill Parcells-led Cowboys in 2003 and by three points in their first game against the Pete Carroll-led Patriots in 1997.
Really, the Jets have too much at stake, even in Week 1, to care much about who the other team’s head coach is. The truth is, even if the Jets win this game, few will change their opinion of how the season will go; the Titans aren’t seen as a quality opponent. But if the Jets lose this game, the noise could turn deafening — and that’s before they head into three straight games of an NFC North gauntlet: home against the Packers, at Lions and at Bears.
Can a Week 1 game be a “must-win”? Probably not. Many teams have overcome a poor Week 1 performance. There’s a reason many in the NFL view the first week as an extension of the preseason.
But for Glenn, that might not matter. A loss on Sunday might feel more apocalyptic than the many that came before it.

Congratulations. If you’re reading this, you’ve made it through the Steelers’ third coaching change since 1969, an offseason of Aaron Rodgers’ indecision, the four-quarterback preseason debates, and the ongoing Joey Porter Jr. negotiations . full_text:
Aaron Rodgers has said it will be his final season, but he's poised for a bigger year than he had in 2025. Dylan Buell / Getty Images
Congratulations. If you’re reading this, you’ve made it through the Steelers’ third coaching change since 1969, an offseason of Aaron Rodgers’ indecision, the four-quarterback preseason debates, and the ongoing Joey Porter Jr. negotiations . As we count down the hours until kickoff, friends and family members keep asking me the same question: “What do you think about the Steelers this year?”
Answering in a few words isn’t easy. Instead, I’ve compiled many of my thoughts into one piece. Here’s what I’m seeing from the Steelers this year.
During training camp last year, Rodgers often had to remind reporters that defenses are usually ahead of the offense. There was no such caveat this season. The chemistry that Rodgers built with his teammates on and off the field, plus the QB’s participation in OTAs, allowed this group to pick up where they left off in 2025.
“I’m extremely confident,” tight end Pat Freiermuth said. “Obviously, going into year two with him, you know what Aaron wants on certain checks and signals and stuff. It’s been a smooth process, honestly. I think a lot of guys are on the same page and playing faster than last year.”
Rodgers’ connection with DK Metcalf, in particular, appears especially strong. Recently, Rodgers was asked about what appears to be an improved supporting cast of pass catchers; he made it clear the offense will still run through the 6-4, 235-pound wideout.
“We got to get the ball to DK,” Rodgers said. “He’s our No. 1 for a reason”
Behind Metcalf, the Steelers’ receiver room appears to be significantly deeper and more talented than it was a season ago. Michael Pittman Jr. has been a legitimate No. 1 receiver at points in his career and will now serve as a possession receiver in a No. 2 role. Roman Wilson has earned significant praise from his QB and head coach. Instead of looking for flashes in camp, he made consistent plays that stood out. And Germie Bernard should eventually be a nice fit in a West Coast offense thanks to his run-after-catch ability and sure hands. There’s optimism — but maybe it’s cautious optimism. Pittman missed several weeks with an undisclosed injury, robbing him of valuable time to build chemistry with Rodgers. Wilson was at least somewhat responsible for Will Howard’s preseason interceptions. Rodgers chastised him last week for not running a route correctly, showing that route details are still an issue. And Bernard is a rookie playing for a QB who demands precision and perfection.
First-round pick Max Iheanachor looked the part during his first two days in pads. The problem: We didn’t see him for several weeks after that as he recovered from an unspecified upper-body injury. That lost time has forced the Steelers to keep Dylan Cook atop the depth chart at right tackle. I don’t expect that to last long. Cook’s performance has been up and down this preseason. When a team has a first-round pick as talented as Iheanachor, they should want to get him on the field as quickly as possible.
Splitting time with Jonnu Smith last year, Freiermuth saw a career-low 51 percent of the offensive snaps. Expect more “Muuuuuuth” chants at Acrisure Stadium this season. Freiermuth’s role in the offense is much clearer with Smith gone. During camp, Rodgers repeatedly looked for Freiermuth over the middle of the field and in two-minute situations. When Rodgers was blitzed in camp, Freiermuth was often the option on vertical routes up the seam. The tight end produced at a near-Pro Bowl level in 2022 (732 yards, 63 receptions). Bold prediction here: This could be the season Freiermuth gets a nod.
“I just really love his versatility,” McCarthy said. “When you get on the field with him and Darnell, both have the ability to play on the line, off the ball. The option routes. Excellent inside route runners. … Pat gives us tremendous flexibility to play one-back and two-back schemes, because he can play the Y, the F, he can get into the backfield, he can play displaced as the No. 1 (outside WR).”
Credit running backs coach Ramon Chinyoung Sr. for coming up with that colorful nickname for the backfield tandem of Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle. It’s also a fitting way to describe what I anticipate the workload to be. Officially, Warren is listed as the top back on the depth chart. But I expect the division of labor to be more even than that document suggests. McCarthy has said that he doesn’t want to have to think about which running back is in the game when he calls plays. Dowdle is more versatile than I anticipated when he was signed. I imagine the Steelers will ride the hot hand, and the leading rusher could change game to game.
I’m also interested to see what Warren can do as a check-down option out of the backfield. As we saw last year, Rodgers often utilized Kenneth Gainwell and leaned on yards after the catch. On 73 catches, Gainwell averaged 7.3 yards after catch per reception, 11th-best in the NFL. Warren led the league with 11.0 yards after catch per reception. He’s lost some weight and appears as shifty as ever.
While you could make the argument that T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Nick Herbig give the Steelers the NFL’s best edge trio, this group has more to prove than their hefty paychecks suggest. Watt’s production has dipped dramatically in the last two seasons. After logging 19 sacks in 2023, he registered 11.5 in 2024 and seven in 2025. Health has been Highsmith’s biggest issue; he has missed 10 games over the last two seasons. And Herbig, who has missed seven games over the last two years, still has something to show on run downs. Can Watt return to his Defensive Player of the Year level (or close to it)? Can Highsmith stay healthy, especially considering he could be on the trading block? And can Herbig make it difficult to take him off the field?
Slowing down Atlanta’s dynamic running back Bijan Robinson is the biggest key to winning in Week 1. Payton Wilson has proven he’s one of the better coverage linebackers in the league. However, he wasn’t able to solidify his spot in the base defense last year because he was inconsistent against the run. He has said he feels like he can play more free this year. Acting on his instincts and using his quick-twitch playing style could help him overcome his lack of bulk. We’ll see how much he’s improved against the run immediately.
If new Steelers defensive coordinator Patrick Graham showed us anything this preseason, it’s that he’s going to be far from vanilla. He’s often used safety rotations and coverage disguises to change the picture for quarterbacks after the snap. In this particular matchup, I’m interested to see how his pressure packages can make life hard on Atlanta. Graham ran the most seven-man pressures in the league last year. While we normally think of blitzes from a passing standpoint, these all-out looks plug every gap and leave running backs with little room to run. It will be interesting to see how much Graham uses a tactic that’s been successful in the past to keep Robinson under wraps.
While we’re talking about Graham, he might be the most important person in defining this team’s ceiling. The Rodgers-McCarthy reunion will be a headline for every prime-time game. However, Graham has the blessing and burden of expectation that comes with coordinating the NFL’s highest-paid defense. I’ve really liked what I’ve seen from Graham schematically on the field. Off the field, I appreciate his authenticity. (He corrected a reporter who said he played at Yale, saying “I was on the team, I didn’t play.”) He’s comfortable in his own skin — and could make quarterbacks quite uncomfortable this year.
To understand what DeShon Elliott’s absence means, look no further than last year. He played at a near-Pro Bowl level in 2024 and the Steelers severely missed him after he went down in Week 8. With the starting strong safety out to begin the…
